subtopic: TABLING OF COPIES OF CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES    PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY

speechtext: Righl Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I should like to lay on the table copies of the convention between Canada and the United States of America for the preservation of the halibut fishery of the northern Pacific ocean and Bering sea, signed at Ottawa today. This happens to be the thirtieth anniversary of the signature for the first time of a treaty on behalf of Canada by Canadians alone. That was the original halibut convention with the United States signed by the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe on March 2, 1923. It seemed fitting that this renewal treaty should be signed by the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and also by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), the son of the signatory of this former treaty in 1923.

subtopic: TABLING OF COPIES OF CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES    PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to ask a question with respect to the statement just made by the Prime Minister in view of the importance of this matter to my constituency and to the Pacific coast. Would it be possible to ask the Minister of Fisheries to indicate what has been accomplished under the treaty and the changes in the new one?

subtopic: TABLING OF COPIES OF CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES    PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext:
The principal achievement, so far as our fishermen are concerned, is in the end result. In 1923 this great fishery on the west coast produced only 15 million pounds of halibut in a full year's fishing by the fleets of both nations. Last year, after thirty years of scientific study and conservation, 62 million pounds were produced by the two fleets in just two months' fishing; that is four times the amount of fish produced in just one-sixth of the time.
A second and equally important result has been the fact that this treaty, which was the first international fisheries treaty in all the world, having been so successful, has been copied by this country and other countries. Here in Canada we have had a succession of international fisheries treaties
all of which are proving extremely successful; they include the international salmon convention for the west coast, the sealing convention and the whaling convention, and the new northwest Atlantic fisheries treaty signed by ten nations to conserve codfish on the Grand Banks. It is because of the fact that we now have several international fisheries treaties that it has been necessary to make the first change in the treaty. The previous treaty was simply called the international fishing convention. There was no other when it was first signed. Now it is to be called the international Pacific halibut convention in order to distinguish it from the other treaties. The United States minister this morning commented on the fact that his country also had used it as a model for other international fisheries treaties they had signed.
The second change is in the number of commissioners. Up till now there were two commissioners from Canada and two from the United States. These commissioners are not paid. In the United States fishing is under the states rather than under the federal government, and the Americans are anxious to give Alaska representation on this commission. So the United States commissioners will represent the federal government, the state of Washington and Alaska. We have agreed, so that each country will have three commissioners.
The only other change is in the open season. The past convention called for one open season and one closed season each year. The scientists' belief is that there are some grounds which could be better utilized if there were different open seasons, and the new convention permits different open seasons to be declared in these great fisheries.

subtopic: SAWMILL AT PETAWAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer orally this question standing in the name of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), and also question No. 54, standing in the name of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), both of which relate to the operation of a sawmill at Camp Petawawa. These questions appeared in Votes and Proceedings for February 26. On February 28, before there had been an opportunity to reply to them, the hon. member for Melfort, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of that date, saw fit to make a number of public allegations charging waste in connection with timber operations at the Petawawa camp.
The facts with respect to the timber operations referred to are as follows:
In the winter of 1950-51 it was considered more economical to carry out lumbering operations on the Petawawa camp properties rather than to purchase lumber in the rising market. Such operations were carried out, and logs were sawn the following summer. This lumber was stockpiled against anticipated requirements. It was considered that this program should continue during the following year and logs to the approximate quantity of 500,000 board feet were cut during the winter of 1951-52 to be sawn the following summer. As a result of reconsideration of this policy, in June of 1952 the operation was discontinued and it was decided to declare surplus the logs then cut and to place the sawmill in storage.
With respect to disposal of the logs Crown Assets Disposal Corporation have advised me as follows:
On July 25,	1952, the Department of
National Defence reported surplus to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation 500,000 feet board measure of jack pine and white pine in logs at Petawawa, Ontario. The declaration was received by the corporation on July 28, 1952, and the availability of this material was circularized to forty-two likely purchasers. Five bids were received. On September 8, 1952, the logs were sold at $29 per 1,000 board feet to the second highest bidder, A. Amyot and Sons, of Hull, Quebec, who put up a deposit of $14,500. The price was in line with the prevailing market.
The highest bid submitted was one of $17,000 received on August 19 from Noik Lumber Company, Pembroke, Ontario but this firm wired on August 26, 1952, that they could not raise the necessary funds and

Questions
cancelled their bid. With respect to the operation of the sawmill, I might say that the declaration of surplus included a right to rent the sawmill which belonged to the Department of National Defence.
On the 15th September, a letter was received from Amyot and Sons requesting authority to rent the army sawmill at Percy Lake and offering to pay as rental $2 per thousand board feet of lumber sawn. This offer was recommended for acceptance and, on the 26th September, Amyot forwarded his cheque in the amount of $1,000 covering the estimated rental and also advising that he had taken steps to insure the mill in the amount of $3,750. Amyot and Sons commenced sawing of logs on the 1st October, 1952, and shut down because of winter weather on 7th November, 1952. The mill has been placed in a state of preservation since that time. Amyot proposes to continue operations in May, 1953.
As will be seen from the foregoing answer to these questions, the allegations made by the hon. member for Melfort as reported in the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, February 28, are not correct. Might I in that connection suggest that if hon. members would avail themselves of the opportunities which exist for securing information from government departments, before hastening to make erroneous charges, the public would be sphred a great deal of inaccurate and misleading information, and public servants would not suffer unfair and unjust criticism.

speechtext: I should like to direct attention to the right hon. Minister of Agriculture. Has he definite information to the effect that the United States embargo against Canadian cattle has been lifted and, if so, what regulations and quotas will apply in the future?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS BY UNITED STATES AND CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is information with regard to the opening of the United States boundary.
The United States today removed the restrictions on the importation of Canadian livestock and meats imposed because of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Canada. The products freed from these restrictions include live cattle, sheep and swine; fresh and cured beef, veal, mutton, lamb and pork; hides and other animal byproducts; hay and straw.
At the same time the Canadian government removed the import controls on livestock and meats, imposed March 1952, to deal with the emergency situation during the period when normal market outlets were closed.
I think probably I should make a little fuller statement than that on the matter, and if the house will permit me I will do so now. It was announced on February 25, 1952, that the animal disease in western Canada was foot-and-mouth disease. The United States government immediately placed an embargo on the importation from Canada of cattle, sheep, or other domestic ruminants, or swine, or of fresh, chilled or frozen beef, veal, mutton, lamb or pork. Restrictions were placed on the importation of cured pork products, hides and other animal by-products, hay and straw. The controls were imposed by means of amendments to bureau of animal industry orders, under the authority of section 306 of the Tariff Act of 1930. On December 13, 1952, the regulations governing the entry of Canadian hay were amended to permit the entry for use as feeding material of Canadian hay produced in an area east .of the 85th meridian west longitude and transported directly to a port in this area.
The intention to declare Canada free of foot-and-mouth disease on March 1, 1953, "if present favourable conditions continue", was announced on November 28, 1952. The announcement, made by the acting secretary of agriculture of the United States, stated that action had been started on regulations

which would permit the entry of Canadian cattle, sheep, other domestic ruminants, and swine, and fresh, chilled or frozen beef, veal, mutton, lamb, or pork. The restrictions applying to other animal products and hay would be removed. On December 6, 1952, a "notice of proposed determination of nonexistence of foot-and-mouth disease in Canada" was published in the Federal Register.
On March 3, 1952, action was taken under the Export and Import Permits Act and the Emergency Powers Act to prohibit, except under permit, the entry of livestock and meat, excluding canned meat-P.C. 1234. This order is being revoked.
During the past year certain measures have been taken under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to prohibit or restrict the entry of certain United States products for sanitary reasons. On May 10, 1952, by ministerial order, the entry from the United States was prohibited of certain fertilizers and feeding stuffs, to reduce the danger of the introduction of anthrax. This order was amended on July 8 to prohibit the import from the United States of (a) bone meal, (b) fertilizers containing bone meal, (c) feeding stuffs containing bone meal intended for consumption by cattle, sheep, goats, other ruminants, swine, horses and poultry. This order is still in effect. On August 29, by ministerial order, the importation was prohibited from the United States of swine, uncooked pork, uncooked pork products, pork offal and garbage. This prohibition, which is still in effect, was imposed because of the prevalence in the United States of vesicular exanthema. Further import requirements for sheep and goats of United States origin were contained in an order in council, P.C. 103, of January 30, 1953, as safeguards against the introduction of scrapie. The new regulations provide that sheep and goats, other than those imported for immediate slaughter, will not be permitted entry unless they are accompanied by a certificate that the animals show no sign of scrapie, that scrapie has not existed on the premises of origin for the three years immediately prior to shipment, and that the animals are not the progeny of a sire or dam that was affected with scrapie or other infectious or contagious disease.
Those are the regulations affected by the order, and also the regulations which will not be affected by the order, which have been brought in recently in order to take care of contagious diseases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the resolution stage of this measure a rather extended discussion took place, and I think the extent of the discussion was such that there is perhaps no need for a repetition of the many arguments to which the minister listened at that time. But I do want to make one or two observations before second reading is carried. The bill of course will not go to the committee of the whole but, as I understand, will be referred to the special committee set up to deal with post office matters and in particular with the question of rural mail service. There is one thing that I hope the minister will make very clear when the committee sits.
Section 24 of the old act is being amended and provision is being made that when the Postmaster General does not accept the lowest tender for a rural mail contract he must report his reasons therefor to the treasury board. I make this suggestion as a guide to the minister when the committee sits. I hope the committee will insist and that the minister will not object to having those reasons made public, if it becomes necessary so far as parliament is concerned, when a contract is questioned in the house at a later time. I only throw that out so that the minister may be prepared for that kind of suggestion when the committee commences its hearings.
I would also like to make a further suggestion to the minister, and I think I made this suggestion perhaps indirectly or obliquely when the matter was before the house in its resolution stage. I hope that, in dealing with rural mail service in general, the suburban mail service may not be forgotten. I know that in the strict terms of reference the committee has to do with rural mail contracts, but, as I pointed out to the minister before, there is a steadily developing problem in suburban areas. I think it has been met partially by the United States government in similar circumstances and I am wondering if perhaps it might not be advisable for the minister, when the committee does commence hearings, to summon someone or to bring satisfactory evidence as to how the question of suburban mail delivery is being handled in the United States in that intermediate stage between rural mail service and letter delivery service. In certain areas in the United States they have problems similar to those we have in Canada.
I must confess that in my reading of the manner in which the United States government deals with that suburban mail delivery I have not been too clear as to exactly how it is worked. I am sure there must be other members in the house who feel as I do, and

we would like to know whether there are some parts of the system in the United States that could be adapted to our particular circumstances in Canada. Those of us who happen to live in rapidly developing areas have problems which perhaps other members may not be fully acquainted with. I do not want to make it a special regional problem but I do hope that when the committee does sit the extent of the reference will be broad and large enough for us to discuss suburban delivery in connection with the rural mail service.
The committee, of course, will deal with these various matters set out in the bill to amend the Post Office Act. I know that the minister is not prepared, and he indicated at the resolution stage he was not prepared, to grant a full investigation into the Post Office Department. I think that would be a very fruitful investigation but I am not going to renew the suggestion. I will say that when the rural mail couriers are brought down here, or their representatives, I hope the minister will not forget that many of these people are working for a small pittance and are having such a difficult time to make ends meet. As a matter of fact, as the minister and others know, the reason for this legislation is that they are not making ends meet. That is why the legislation is here and I hope that some provision will be made to hear representatives of the rural mail couriers from various parts of Canada. They should not have to come here at their own expense-they could not afford to do so-and if we ask them to come at their own expense it will be tantamount to refusing them a hearing altogether.
I do not know what the general procedure is in connection with committees of that kind, regarding the subpoenaing of witnesses, and whether their expenses are paid; but I do hope that special consideration will be given to the rural mail couriers. I do not think we should just hear technical experts about rural mail. I think we -should hear from at least the odd one of our rural mail men, men who actually have to carry the mail themselves under these conditions which, as best we can, we are trying to remedy.
I am not suggesting to the minister that many of them should come here; I would not suggest that for a moment. But enough rural mail couriers should be brought here to give evidence so that we may have a fairly true, accurate and full picture of what the problems are in the various regions where the rural mail couriers carry on their work.
In addition, I hope that, when the committee does sit, full consideration will be given to every angle of the changes that are
Post Office Act
suggested. We might as well speak frankly about it and not put any false face upon the problem that we face. We have got to find some way of at least giving some equity to the people who carry the rural mail. At the same time, we must avoid putting them in the position where there will likely be any patronage abuses in connection with the system. I can quite understand that the minister will be anxious, of course, not to have too much responsibility left on his doorstep in certain cases. But there might be some minister at some time who would welcome some responsibility with respect to the manner in which these contracts might be changed from time to time. I can only point out that I have been between two fires in my thinking, as far as this is concerned. I want to help the rural mail couriers on the one hand, but I do not want the rural mail couriers to get into the clutches of somebody who might conceivably have some little party political interest in mind. As I look across the chamber here I cannot conceive of anyone there that would have such a thought- particularly at this stage of our parliament. In any event, I do want to suggest that in our committee sessions we will have to avoid that feature very carefully. I may say that we are very anxious, when we take office, not to have in our power anything that would perhaps be regarded as something which could be abused. We are anxious to see that the rural mail courier gets a square deal and that he shall not have to vote in a particular way in order to get it. I think that ought to be the general belief and the general policy of our committee as a whole.
In giving consent to second reading of this bill-and I fancy there will be no division in connection with it at this time, because I do not suppose any of us are in a very good position to say whether this bill ought to be passed or ought to be approved at the moment-I think all of us will welcome the committee's fact-finding adventure. When we get the facts and when we have the evidence fairly in front of us then we will, of course, be in a better position to judge whether this bill ought to be endorsed in principle or not. In the meantime, I think it ought to go before the committee, and I for one will only be too glad to see it get there at the earliest possible moment.
I suggest that when the committee is set up those who are sitting on the committee should park their party divisions outside the door and do a job for the rural mail couriers, because this, I think, is one problem that for a long time has almost baffled solution by people on all sides of the house. I am hopeful that when this committee brings in its decision with respect to the rural mail

Post Office Act
couriers we will not have this evergreen debate year in and year out regarding the rural mail couriers' problems.
I think everyone will welcome some kind of a finale to the problem and to the inequities which have existed so long in connection with the work of such an important section of our Canadian people in the public service.
I would hope that this would be a very fruitful committee and I take it that the house will be prepared to give second reading to the bill in order that we may then be in a position to learn the facts that this committee will no doubt bring to the house.

speechtext:
I am pleased to support the second reading of this bill, and its reference to a committee of this house. I feel that the provision in the bill

which permits an upward adjustment of carrier contracts is a good one. It seems to me that the rates in many contracts are extremely low. It is only fair that some provision be made for an upward adjustment in the rates, so that carriers may be paid a reasonable amount for this essential service.
The provision that contracts for under $1,000 shall be let without tender perhaps leaves the door open for the accusation of patronage. On the other hand, I feel that if that provision were used fairly and equitably it could result in an improvement for the rural mail carriers. It seems to me that the amounts that are paid for this service are sometimes too low. When a service is open for contract a number of people who need some additional money very badly will underbid one another until the person who gets the contract perhaps makes little or nothing out of it. I would suggest that the committee might consider some kind of formula. I believe it has already been suggested that a mileage rate might be established, perhaps based on the topography, the type of highway and so on, in the area. If something could be spelled out that perhaps would not fix the remuneration but at least might serve as a guide to what would be fair and equitable for a certain job, it would be useful.
We might divide the country into various sections. I imagine a rate, for example, could be worked out that would be fair for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, because within those three provinces the conditions which a mail carrier must face are quite similar. I would think that a departmental committee might be set up for the purpose of considering applications for contracts. In that consideration I would give high preference to veterans requesting a contract. I would give considerable weight to an applicant who had a family to maintain. I would give him additional consideration if his other income was very low. I can think of young people starting in business or starting on a farm who could very well use some additional income. I believe, therefore, that in determining to whom a contract will be given, where that contract is for less than $1,000, some consideration should be given to the needs of the person applying.
Naturally, you would have to investigate each applicant to see that he could put forward the necessary guarantee that the service would be carried out. There are other types of individual contracts that are made after the applications have been processed by a committee on the basis of need. I know that the provisions of this bill may increase the possibility of patronage. It seems to
Post Office Act
me that there is a lot of consideration being given to the early passage of this bill. Perhaps it has something to do with the imminence of a general election; I am not sure. In any case, I am pleased to lend my support to this bill, as I think the provisions are reasonable if contracts are let after due consideration of the various points I have mentioned. I believe if that were done it would result in definite improvement in the lot of our rural mail carriers.

want to say that I am in favour of the passage of this bill. However, there are a few items in it which I should like to briefly draw to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), with particular reference to my constituency. We find that one of the amendments in this bill gives to the Postmaster General the right to settle contracts for less than $1,000, but he must do that on a basis comparable to the services already existing in that area. Therefore, before deciding on the $1,000 one or less, he will have to take into consideration how it compares with other contracts already in existence in that constituency. For instance, let us take the situation in a constituency that I myself know. In that constituency there are 106 contracts to be let. With the passing of this act the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) is given almost absolute control, inasmuch as he would control about 75 or 80 of those contracts, unless he is going to compare them with other contracts; and if so, then surely they would step up beyond the $1,000 mark.
In connection with the letting of those contracts I can also see this situation unless this part of the bill is carried into effect, namely, that the services under the contracts must be comparable to the services in other parts of the district. For instance, in our district I have always complained about the terrible discrimination with regard to these contracts. Instead of the situation getting better, I find that it has been getting worse. For instance we find one man, driving a distance of 15J miles and serving 46 boxes, who gets $1,500; while two other mail couriers, or probably four or five, drive twice that distance-that is 30 miles-and the Postmaster General says to them: "You have got to serve 126 boxes but we are going to give you $110 less than the man who is driving 15J miles." Those are things that, when he has this committee, I think the Postmaster General should go into. I believe he should try to get a fair wage scale for those people who are carrying the mail. I could go on, as I have done before, and put on record what has happened in specific cases. Many of these

Post Office Act
cases should be looked into by this committee that is appointed and which should be functioning fairly soon.
Another thing that I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General is this. Where a contract is to be let and tenders are equal-say $1,200 for each contract -what will be the procedure under this amendment? Will they go back and will new tenders be called, or will the Postmaster General reserve the right to give the contract to whomever he desires if the tender is accepted in the amount of $1,200? At the present time I think that in most cases when tenders are equal, are $1,000 or over and have been turned back, it is the only time that the representative in that constituency, whoever he may be, gets an opportunity of naming the man whose tender will be accepted.
Another matter that I should like to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General and which I think should come before this committee is that of the extra help at the Christmas season and the pay that this extra help gets. There is no other time in the whole year, in the service of the Post Office Department, when the extra help employed work harder than they do at Christmas time. They work harder then than at any other time in the year. They work longer hours and are busy all the time. They are not paid a fair wage. In some places we find that they have been receiving as high as 85 cents an hour while in other postal areas the rate goes down as low as 65 cents an hour. They should be placed on a fair wage per hour all over, because they all work about the same number of hours, engage in the same kind of work, and are obliged to work very hard indeed. Any extra help in other departments of government, no matter what they are, get wages higher than 85 cents an hour and I do not think we should discriminate against the extra helpers who are working so hard in order to get the mail out during the Christmas season.
I am not going to take up more time because I know the Postmaster General is anxious to get this bill through; but, as I said before, there are a few items like those I have mentioned that I should like to see the Postmaster General take up with his own committee so that we may get something fair and equitable for the rural mail couriers across Canada. We all know that they have not been fairly dealt with. In fact, they are not getting even a fair wage today in comparison with that of other classes of employees.

Mr. Speaker, in generally supporting this bill may I say that I am glad that the committee is going
[Mr. McLure.l
to be set up, before which the members of the various post office workers' organizations will be able to appear. The nature of the work of the post office is such that, although these workers occasionally approach their members of parliament, I am afraid that- speaking frankly for myself-the average layman has difficulty in understanding the technical problems. For that reason I am glad they will have a place in which to appear, where the deputy postmaster general and other experts in this work will be present who will be qualified to judge of the various representations which they care to make.
The reason I rose to my feet, Mr. Speaker, was that the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) I thought wisely suggested that the reference to the committee might be broadened to take in some of the problems of the people who live in suburban areas; that is to say the deliveries in suburban areas. One can understand the difficulty where new territory on the outskirts of a city grows up quickly and thus creates a special problem. It is about the special problem in my constituency that I just want to say a word at the moment, because I believe it is time that it should be given some consideration.
I am informed-I do not know how correctly-that in certain of these crowded suburban areas, while they have no delivery as such from the, shall I say, branch post office, nevertheless special couriers or workers are sent out from the central office and that they put in time on this work. It may not take them a full day but they deliver the mail in those areas and to all intents and purposes, so far as the residents of the community are concerned, that is just as good as if they had a delivery of their own. I am thinking particularly of the people in the little town of Sutherland who, I expect, would rather resent it if I said they were a suburban area of the city of Saskatoon. Nevertheless they are there. The two places are getting so that they almost touch each other, and there is a first class cement road connecting them. May I say that the population is growing fast, and that it is not scattered. For purposes of delivery, I think the suggestion I make is a very good one. If at the moment conditions in Sutherland are not such as to justify the setting up of door-to-door delivery, perhaps arrangements could be made whereby delivery could be carried out from the city of Saskatoon.
I am not an expert in these matters, but I have had this suggestion made to me by a correspondent who lives in Sutherland but who works in Saskatoon. A good many of the people living in this little town do work

in the adjacent city. Quite often however they find it more convenient to have their mail delivered at the city office than to pick it up in their own home town. During the course of the day, perhaps at the lunch hour, a person could call at the city post office and obtain his mail in that way. If this is done, he will have his mail with him when he goes home. On the other hand, if it is not done that way, he may have to make an extra trip, when he returns to Sutherland, to get his mail.
This was done by one or two people, and the Post Office Department found it out. It was learned that non-residents of the Saskatoon area would have to pay $6 for a box, whereas they would get a box in Sutherland for $2. I am sure more people would be getting their mail in Saskatoon if that were not the case. They find, however, that by getting their mail at the city office they have to pay a higher fee for the box.
I draw this matter to the minister's attention, in the hope that there may be some discussion in committee concerning an arrangement of some kind whereby delivery of the kind I have indicated would be permitted, not from the small town post office but from the main post office in the adjacent city. I do not know what the demand is for mail delivery in Sutherland at the moment, but it has occurred to me that an arrangement of the kind I have suggested might be brought into being.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to only one matter which I mentioned before when this subject was before the house. It is my contention that within the bill there may be provisions for removing some of the bugs, as we call them, from the old system of mail delivery. However, there is one practice I would like to see stopped, and that is the practice of acquiring contracts and then subletting them. Certainly certain evils have arisen as a consequence of this procedure.
Persons bid on contracts and secure them at relatively low figures. Then there are always people who find themselves in circumstances where they are compelled to take the contracts at $100 or $200 less than the prices at which the contracts were secured. This results in these poor devils, if I may use that unparliamentary expression, undertaking to carry the mail at a ridiculously low figure.
When the minister's department lets a contract it is my contention that the person who takes the contract should have the facilities to carry the mail, and also the intention of carrying it, rather than subletting it. This practice of subletting should be discouraged,

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for the budget speech he made in this house not long ago. Yet, it has been received by the great majority as a good budget, a businessman's budget, the budget of a man who completely understands the workings of a national economy; the budget of a man who knows he is administering public funds, that the money he is called upon to distribute as treasurer of the nation is derived from the taxpayers of Canada as a whole. There is one thing which I notice quite often. The opposition clamours for a reduction in expenses and, at the same time, a reduction in taxes. In the very same effort, they request new expenditures from the government.
I remember

and I know that the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), who is doing me the honour of listening to what I have to say at this moment, also recalls the Roberval election. On that occasion the present member for Roberval (Mr. Spence) had published an electoral pamphlet, in which one could read in article 5-he was speaking to the Roberval electorate-
That you want the government to help the farmers as it did in the case of the western farmers -Gardiner gave them $65 million last year.
It is in these words that the hon. member was addressing his electors and the member for Three Rivers was one of his most emphatic comrades in arms-I do not want to offend his modesty in saying that he was one of the ablest-but these two gentlemen have voted twice in favour of devoting some $200 million to a project in Saskatchewan. They said it was too much to give them $65 million, but they are ready to give them more than $200 million. For some time I have been wondering whether the "brain trust" is working as it should.
FMr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1

Now, Mr. Speaker, it is said that the personal income tax has not been sufficiently reduced. Well, I must say that the Minister of Finance has managed to reduce it.
On the* other hand, the Minister of Finance found a way of reducing the personal income tax. In fact, if the hon. gentlemen of the opposition would study closely the events which have taken place since 1945, they would see that the Minister of Finance has lightened the taxation burden by $65 million; for the taxpayers would have to pay $65 million as an annual interest on the debt. They no longer need do so as the debt has been reduced by 30 per cent, that is to say by more than $2 billion, since 1945. That represents a worth while tax reduction. But our hon. friends seem to have a telescope which they use by looking through the large end, rather than through the small one-which is unusual.
On the other hand, the personal income tax has decreased by 11 per cent. The tax on cigarettes has been reduced by 4 cents. True, in Quebec-I do not know if it is in order to safeguard provincial autonomy-half a cent has been added, once the budget had been brought down, so that, in the province of Quebec, cigarettes are 4 cents more expensive than in Ontario. I met a few constituents right after the budget had been brought down and they said "You're buying your cigarettes in Ontario?" I said yes, adding that I paid 4 and even 5 cents less for a pack of 25 cigarettes; that is again due to Mr. Duplessis' tax. As in the case of the gasoline tax, he hastened to put it back, as soon as the federal government had removed it.
This year, the federal government is decreasing taxes by about $300 million. The stamp tax on cheques and postal orders, which was considered a nuisance tax, is removed, and everyone knows how much it annoyed the public. The famous radio licence also goes. The first electors I met right after the budget had been brought down said to me, "The radio licence has gone, at last." Also the exemptions are doubled with regard to dividends paid by Canadian companies. And the limit provided as regards deduction of medical expenses for income tax purposes is lowered from 4 to 3 per cent.
Now, I was surprised, the other day, to hear the hon. member for Roberval say that only very few people would benefit from the deduction allowed for children over 21 years of age who attend a university. Mr. Speaker, I do say a good many French-Canadian fathers, numerous farmers and many workers who send their children to universities and who believe in the necessity of education and

instruction, will undoubtedly avail themselves of this exemption. I know that many fathers do thank the government for this deduction. I hope that in this case the Minister of Finance in no way interfered with provincial autonomy when he decided to allow that reduction and to authorize the head of a family to take advantage of the tax deduction granted in the case of children who go to a university.
There is also the 10 per cent sales tax deduction on low-priced books. That is another point which is rather important and proper in the eyes of the people of Quebec who are interested not only in Canadian literature but also in foreign and particularly in French literature.
I have already pointed out, Mr. Speaker, the 30 per cent reduction in our national debt and the fact that we now pay $65 million less in interest annually. After all, that is something, Mr. Speaker, and when I spoke of the exemption granted to fathers with dependent children over 21 years of age attending university, of course I used the words provincial autonomy.
Countless speeches have been made on the subject of autonomy, especially in the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I am an autonomist. The first time I asked the population of Portneuf county to elect me, I did so for the sake of my county's autonomy.
It is very well to speak of autonomy but one has to give the example. When the premier of Quebec talks about provincial autonomy, he should at the same time remember that taxpayers in his province have also a right to autonomy. His Bill No. 34, amending the elections act, is certainly one of the most grievous attacks which could be made upon the autonomy of the elector. This Bill No. 34 is certainly an encroachment on the voters' autonomy. I abstain from mentioning the autonomy of our school and municipal boards in the province of Quebec.
I understand it has often been said in the province of Quebec that Mr. Frost had been taken by the throat. But Mr. Frost has stated-I have already quoted in the house this clipping from L'Action Catholique of October 21, 1952, according to which Mr. Frost said in the Ontario legislature:
In the circumstances Ontario has not sacrificed any of its constitutional rights.
That is clear, that is absolutely evident and anyone who examines the situation objectively can see that the federal government never took Mr. Frost by the throat.
The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier
The province of Quebec is losing a good deal of money on account of autonomy. The other day, I heard a speaker say: We do not want to sell our freedom in exchange for federal grants. Words like that may have some electoral effect when spoken on the hustings, but I believe a man should think it over seriously before uttering words like that.
Since 1867, the question of autonomy has often been mentioned and is often brought up. However, in the province of Quebec, we still speak French, sing in French, and we are still practising the same religion as our ancestors did. We actually believe that, even though the federal anti-autonomists, as they are called-and efforts are being made most of the time to describe the present federal government as a foreign government; the word may be strong but it is the word they use-hold to the contrary in spite of all that, there still exist in that province those who still occupy a rank very close to the top, if not the very first rank. I have much confidence in the present government, and at all events, I don't think that the danger of losing all our constitutional rights in the province of Quebec is that ominous at the present time.
There may be people in this country who foster centralization, who don't believe in autonomy as much as we do in the province of Quebec, and I understand them, because they are not in the same position as we are with regard to language, institutions, our civil code and our religion, but, at all events, this government and the present Prime Minister, more than any of the premiers of the various provinces, have given proof that they are in favour of provincial autonomy.
Besides, one thing is reassuring, and that is that our present Prime Minister is sincere when he speaks, his thinking is clear and precise; he speaks objectively and in such a way that we always know where he stands. That is all the difference which exists between a man who understands and puts in its proper perspective the subject he is talking about, and the one who makes of it a political football.
Mr. Speaker, it will possibly appear as though I wish to raise points which have little to do with the budget, but I believe references were made to federal-provincial relations in the budget speech and I have the right to dot my "i's", because it happens too often that in our province we hear grandiloquent speeches about autonomy which are mainly intended for the public. I know that some are sincere, but unfortunately there are still too many who use it as a political springboard. That is why I will speak about it today.

The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier
The other day the attitude of Mr. Taschereau and of the Hon. Mr. Lapointe at the Quebec Reform Club in 1920 was quoted. These gentlemen were autonomists. They did not shout as long as the present Quebec premier, but they worked harder, more objectively, with neutral glasses, not with red or blue ones. With neutral glasses they looked at the problem, putting it in its proper perspective. They caused our provincial autonomy to take a giant stride forward. They preserved our constitutional liberties in a far more certain fashion than any ordinary politician could. I do not understand very well why certain provincial politicians in the province of Quebec take the stand they do.
If I look back a little, I recall the Bilodeau-Rogers agreement, passed several years ago-

The federal government placed $2 million at the disposal of the minister of social welfare and of youth, but the thing is being hushed. Besides, Mr. Speaker, I have here a sheet entitled-
Classification of the yearly contributions and grants for capital expenses, paid to the province of Quebec, under the terms of the agreement concerning aid to technical schools.
It goes back to 1945 and I see here that the Montreal technical school, which belongs in a way to the technical schools of the educational system, has been granted, since 1945, $206,250 for building purposes and $66,000 for equipment. The Quebec technical school was granted $204,500 for building purposes and $99,345 for equipment. speechtext:
One moment. The Hull technical school, $97,500 for building purposes and $18,000 for equipment. As for the Sherbrooke technical school, $162,000 for building purposes and $45,000 for equipment.
After all, it is something. The province of Quebec carries on with its education according to the program set up by the committee of education. I think that the encroachment on its autonomy is not very great.
Yet these agreements were signed by Union Nationale governments and, as I said just now, we are losing quite a lot of money because of this appeal for autonomy. And I shall prove it.
I have here the answer given by the hon. Mr. Winters to a question by Mr. Follwell. I am quoting from page 2384 of Hansard for February 25, 1953:
1.	What has been the total cost to the federal government of the trans-Canada highway?
I'll spare you the remainder of the question, but shall give you the answer to No. 1:
1. Totals to February 14, 1953: Provincial commitments, $95,075,540.71; Canada's share, $47,537,770.35; Paid to provinces, $28,319,916.54.
Then we see, under No. 2, the payments made to the various provinces by the federal government. It can be seen that the province of Ontario has received $10,295,333.15, and the province of Quebec, nothing. That is to say, Mr. Speaker, that under the pretext of safeguarding its autonomy, the province of Quebec refuses federal help towards the construction of the trans-Canada highway, whereas Ontario is getting more than $10 million. When the federal government calls upon the provincial governments to fulfil an obligation which is reasonable, sensible and decent, when it asks them to request tenders for road construction and repairs, I do not see how serious people can pretend that it affects provincial autonomy. It is for that reason that the government of the province of Quebec has refused to sign an agreement with the federal government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before proceeding further I want to thank the government for having designated an ambassador to Spain. This was no mere whim on my part, Mr. Speaker; my wish was based on arguments which I thought serious enough and which I have exposed several times in this house since 1945.
Spain is a country with a very high culture; owing to the character of its people and to its religion, Spain stands as one of the most solid bulwarks against the spread of

communism in the whole world and more particularly in the other countries where Spanish culture has flourished, as in South America for instance.
Moreover, I have always claimed that Spain, on account of its important situation in the Mediterranean, would increase greatly our security since it could safeguard the free and permanent movement of English ships which sail through the Mediterranean and the Suez canal, so that the allies may trade more easily with the countries of the south, of Africa and of Asia.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to say a few words on a subject which was brought up the other day by the member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) when he took the Leader of the Opposition to task and reminded him of what he had said about family allowances. I do not want to repeat uselessly anything on the subject because I am sure that public opinion is quite definite in that respect. I would like however to quote what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert said on February 27, 1953, as reported on page 2478 of Hansard:
Speaking of old speeches by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), as a member from the Atlantic provinces, having regard to the fact that through this social security measure we get back some share of the profits which we send to other parts of Canada, I for one am not going to let the mothers of the Atlantic provinces forget that the Leader of the Opposition said that the family allowances bill was wicked and unjust.
The hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) then asked him:
How long ago was that?
I know that it was a long time ago, Mr. Speaker, that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke that way. In that connection, I wish to recall a saying that goes like this: God deliver me from my friends and I shall myself look after my enemies. The Leader of the Opposition should keep that saying in mind. I have here an item from the Toronto Star-a paper I read every night following the adjournment of the house. It quotes the Globe and Mail which attacks the social security legislation of the Liberal government. If my information is correct, that newspaper befriends the opposition and the leader of the Conservative party. The item I am quoting is dated February 23, 1953: (Text):
The Globe and Mail says it has discovered "the greatest weakness of the budget-one that has developed to an alarming point under cover of past surpluses."
And what is this alleged weakness? The Globe answers: "A large part of present-day budgets goes not to defence but to progressive expenditures (notably welfare expenditures) which depend on percentage taxes."
The Budget-Mr. R Gauthier (Translation):
It shows that the present opposition has always had some kind of grudge against the social security legislation, which, after all, includes family allowances.
Now, going further back, in 1951, the Globe and Mail, still quoted by the Toronto Star, had this to say:
(Text):
It may even prove wise for the Minister of Finance at this time to weigh against an increase in taxation a substantial measure of budget economy such as the suspension of the family allowances.
Those are the words of the opposition.
At present 1,852,000 families receive these monthly cheques which over a year amount to $300 million. This is a large dollop-
And do not overlook those words.
-to take off a budget and its loss would do harm to no one.
That is the writing of the Globe and Mail.
A little further on, in October, 1952, the Globe and Mail has this to say:
Are we to suppose that up until 1945, when the so-called social security program came into effect, the needy got no help? Are we to suppose that if that program were abolished the poor would be allowed to die in the gutter? Is compassion only to be found among Liberal politicians? To paraphrase Mr. Churchill on a famous occasion, what kind of people does the Star think we are?
(Translation) :
And so, Mr. Speaker, these are the words and the writings of the official opposition's friends. When we are asked to forget the words of its leaders, we of course tell ourselves that he has obviously changed his mind. But here we have his friends, and the most powerful among his friends, who carry out consistently more open attacks-though sometimes these attacks are carried out more discreetly

on the social security legislation which includes, among other things, family allowances.
And, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert put it:
I for one am not going to let the mothers of the Atlantic provinces forget that the Leader of the Opposition said that the family allowances bill was wicked and unjust.
Mr. Speaker, I will not allow it to be forgotten myself. I will not forget, either, that our mothers have been empire builders, as we call them in the province of Quebec. But here they have been publicly insulted by a public figure. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that family allowance legislation has been extremely popular, because of the fact that it touches upon the very existence of the family.

The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier It is true that they all live for one another and all for the home. Canada, Mr. Speaker, is like a family and if a part of Canada is affected, the whole, country is concerned. The province of Quebec is not the only one to benefit from family allowances; all the other provinces also benefit from it. And I believe that the way the Liberal government has been concerned with the welfare of the Canadian families cannot be forgotten. Politicians should cease opposing the maintenance of this legislation; otherwise they would make a false move, a serious mistake, and prove that they don't understand how important is the Canadian family.
The Canadian family is important, especially when we have to fight the communist theories. That is what helps us maintain our freedom, and it is thanks to our families that we have been able to keep our unity.
Mr. Speaker, I also wished to refer to a more restricted field, that of family farms. In Quebec, we have family farms and the acreage of these farms is smaller than in the western provinces. The average farm in the province of Quebec, let us say of 100 to 250 acres, which is good enough for a family farm, compares favourably with those of Ontario and New Brunswick. On the other hand, in the western provinces, especially in Saskatchewan, there seems to be a tendency to monopolization, which is becoming a danger in the neighbouring country, especially in the southern part of the United States where the majority of farms have become farming industries rather than agricultural farms. I have here the figures on the American agricultural census for 1945. You will note, Mr. Speaker, the centralization of acreage in the farms of the southern states. The number of farms of more than 1,000 acres in 1900 was 47,160, and in 1947 it was 112,899. That means that in 1900 the percentage of farms of over a thousand acres, in the United States, was 0-8, and that in 1947 it was 1-9.
I see in volume 2 of the same census that 38 per cent of all farms in the United States which are not over 50 acres represented only 4-1 per cent of the total area of all arable land in the whole United States.
That shows how centralization of farming land has progressed in the United States; as a matter of fact, it is falling into the hands of a few people. We do not want that to happen in the province of Quebec, for we realize that the family farm in Quebec province, as in France, is perhaps the most solid foundation which a national economy can have.
May I be allowed to remind you, Mr. speaker, that when in 1871, Germany compelled France to pay her 5 billion francs in 
reparations, it was France's well-lined stocking which allowed her to meet her obligations; so when we speak of the family farms in Quebec and think of all those personal savings which, in France, were so useful to the mother country, it is easy to understand why we are so attached to our family farms.
I shall quote some figures about family farms in the province of Quebec. In 1901, farms situated on 1 to 10 acres of land represented a proportion of 9-7 per cent; on 11 to 50 acres of land, 14-3 per cent; from 51 to 100 acres, 32-7 per cent; from 101 to 200 acres, 31-6 per cent; as for farms situated on 201 acres of land and more, they represented but 11-7 per cent.
According to the data given to me by the Quebec bureau of statistics, since 1941 things have not changed much, the number of family farms having varied but little, from an acreage standpoint. In 1941, 2-8 per cent of farms still had 1 to 10 acres; 12-2 per cent, from 11 to 50 acres, a group which, in 1901, represented a percentage of 14-3 and thus saw its percentage fall. Farms on 51 to 100 acres of land reached a percentage of 39-1; the proportion for farms of 101 to 200 acres was 34-3 while in 1901 it was 31-6 per cent.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the proportion of farms of 101 to 200 acres has not increased very much, only 3 per cent from 1901 to 1941 in the province of Quebec. That is to say that the system of farms operated on a family basis is being maintained in the province of Quebec. We are asking protection for the family farms of Quebec because we believe they constitute the strongest foundation we can have. Anyone who looks objectively at the situation readily sees that the federal government is thinking of the family farms of Quebec. One only has to look at the statistics I have just quoted to be convinced.
Last year the federal government paid over $7 million-$7,616,770.42 to be exact-in the province of Quebec, in the form of subsidies for the transport of grain from western to eastern Canada. Since that legislation was passed, some $69 million have been paid for the transport of grain.
That shows that the government is looking after the agricultural family in the province of Quebec, and this government should be proud of that policy.
I could quote other figures to show how much this government is concerned with the economy of the province of Quebec, as it is with the economy of all the provinces. But, we know that the population of this

country is only 14 million, that it is an immense country, not easy to run, and that the government has to endeavour to meet the various interests of the different provinces in order to maintain the economic unity of the whole country. And, moreover, it must keep the country united and its achievements in that connection speak for themselves. This reminds me of a sentence written by Graham Spry, I believe, which describes Canada as-
A nation, two cultures; a loyalty, two races; two glorious pasts, one future.
Mr. Speaker, that is how the member for Portneuf considers Canada. Oh, going through my former speeches, one may find rather bitter and violent words, relating to certain statements of mine. Still, I remind myself of something Abraham Lincoln once
The Budget-Mr. P. Gauthier said: I know of no man wise enough today not to be wiser the next day.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I congratulated the government for looking into the problems of the province of Quebec and more especially of the French-Canadian families and family farms. In other provinces such as Saskatchewan, Alberta or Manitoba, the centralizing tendencies for farms is stronger than in Quebec, Ontario or New Brunswick. The situation is different there.

I wanted to tell you that in Quebec, we attach great importance to social security legislation, such as family allowances or old age pensions, which after all were adopted by the federal government as a result of agreements with the provinces. I fail to see that provincial autonomy has been affected thereby. I add that thought to what I was saying a while ago on the question of the Rogers agreements.

Mr. Speaker, I could not entirely follow the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, for obvious reasons, although I could understand and follow him in part of that which he said.
I want to discuss for a little while some phases of the budget, and matters to which I think more attention should have been paid. One thing which certainly can be said with respect to this budget is that never before have the drums of propaganda or, perhaps I should say, the guns of propaganda been so cocked and primed as they were for this one. The papers were filled the next day with photographs of jubilant people standing in front of the cash registers and getting cigarettes at prices at which we could not get them here in the government buildings. Those of us who had sometimes wondered where the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had been during the week or two before he presented this budget, thinking that he had been working very hard on its preparation, after seeing the pictures in the paper next day judged that he must have spent most of his time in having his photograph taken; because down in the east, where we have to work very hard, in the Halifax Herald the minister is portrayed in his shirtsleeves-

It is a complimentary picture of the hon. gentleman. As he moved nearer to the centre of Canada he became more effete and more insouciant in his appearance, in handing out cancelled stamps and other matters. But on hearing the propaganda and reading it in the press, one could not help thinking that after all the poorer

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan the product, the more salesmanship is required in order to put it over. You do not need any gilt to paint a gold brick, but you do need it to paint a copper brick if it is to be portrayed as gold. I think that is the effort that was made in this case, and perhaps not too successfully because I am sure it has boomeranged.
There was a great deal of talk in the press about the jubilant government benches on the night of the delivery of the budget. I think that is a reasonably fair statement. When the Minister of Finance was speaking of the iron ore of Labrador, the oils of Alberta and the aluminum of British Columbia, I thought that Divine Providence came in for a tremendously greater amount of praise and applause than did the minister himself, when he announced his tax reductions. I thought those were greeted with much less applause than were the tributes to the bounteous wealth of this nation from which we derive a great deal of our prosperity and for which the government apparently is taking much of the credit at the moment.
We have also seen the references to the gloomy looks that were on the faces of the Tories over here when they listened to the wonderful words of the minister. Mr. Speaker, we poor fellows did not even know we looked sad. As a matter of fact, we did not feel that way at all.

speechtext: You look that way all the time.

maintopic: NUMBER OF OCCUPIED FARMS, VALUE OF PRODUCTS SOLD, AND FARMS CLASSIFIED BY SIZE OF FARM
speechtext:
We may look that way all the time. After all, we get kicked around a great deal by this government. We perhaps have some reason for looking a little bit sad at times. I know that the fishermen down on the east coast have a far-away look in their eyes and are a little bit sad, waiting as they are for the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) to come down there and do something more for them than has been done hitherto. There is good reason for their being sad, as I will suggest to the minister in a moment.
However, we did not know that we looked sad on that occasion. We knew that we were listening to a minister of finance who had, throughout the years, taken away a million dollars a day in surpluses for almost every day during which he had been minister; and we expected that there would be substantial tax reductions to the people of Canada when this his last budget-or presumably so, according to press reports-was being presented. We knew that we were facing a government which, by reasonable economies, could curtail the expenditures of this nation greatly, and we expected to hear of something of that kind.

With those two factors in the background we thought there would be a substantial reduction in taxation, and we were prepared for it. If we looked so sad, Mr. Speaker, as some of our friends have suggested, the only reason I can suggest for it is that we must have been feeling sorry for the taxpayers rather than for ourselves; because I can assure you, sir, that we did not feel sorry for ourselves, and I do not think we are at the moment.
After all, what does this budget do? If the Minister of Finance had come before the house frankly and said that this was a businessman's budget, a budget for businessmen,
I think he would at least have been entitled to credit for his frankness. Although the budget might have been open to criticism on various grounds, I think at least he could not be accused of trying to guild the gold brick or to paint a lily where no lily existed. But of course that was a rather difficult course for this government to take. This party or this government which calls itself Liberal, which has been here for so many years, and which has become a sort of political dinosaur, as it has crawled down the government road sometimes veered to the left and sometimes to the right. This time it took a sharp turn to the right; it got away from the left side of the road and headed far over on the right. Of course that could not be admitted because, after all, this is something which must be for all the people and not just for perhaps the business interests.
So the minister was heralded as having been the giver of great gifts. From reading the speeches, the propaganda and even the editorials at the beginning, one would have thought that the budget combined all the generosity of the Marshall plan, the Point Four program of Mr. Truman, and the Colombo plan thrown in for good measure. Actually it gave reductions to certain classes of people, and only on a limited scale. The minister does not make a good Santa Claus, Mr. Speaker. He is described as genial and debonair and dashing. With all those qualifications, descriptions and appellations we will agree. But when he tries to come into this house carrying a Santa Claus pack on his back and to be portrayed as distributing largesse to the taxpayers generally, may I say that he did not do such a good job at it. After all, the few presents he had in his sack still carried the sales tax label upon them; and he was standing fairly well in the shadows of extravagance and wastefulness so we could not see too well just what it was that he was distributing.
With many of those reductions we on this side of the house agree. In fact, in many

cases we have urged those reductions. It is highly satisfactory to see that matters which we have recommended in the past, such as abolition of the radio fee and reductions in other taxes, have been accepted by this government and by the Minister of Finance. The financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), and others have dealt with those matters fairly extensively, and I am not going to attempt to elaborate upon what they have said.
I think, generally speaking, we have levelled two criticisms at this budget. When the Klieg lights of the propaganda machine have been turned off, what does the ordinary taxpayer find? Well, of course those who wish to smoke their way to prosperity find that reductions have been made for them which, of course, are undoubtedly appreciated. Then the individual income taxpayer has received varying degrees of relief. Those on the lower scale, however, received very little indeed.
We are told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that these tax reductions amount to 11 per cent, and then he qualifies his statement by saying that, of course, it is 11 per cent for the full year, and only 5J per cent for this year. But he suggests that we look forward to the next year, and that possibly we will get the 11 per cent reduction. Let me say, in parentheses, that anyone who takes the promise of tax reductions by this government for more than a year in advance is certainly very much of an optimist, because we have had more than one instance of taxation being changed in the middle of the year. I do not think anyone can look forward with any great degree of certainty to what may take place in the coming year.
After all, as has been pointed out, it is not 5J per cent for this year. Why the Minister of Finance persists in his description of this as a 5J per cent reduction, and excludes from it the social security tax, is more than the ordinary individual can understand. It is true that that tax is earmarked for a certain purpose. But, Mr. Speaker, it comes out of your pocket and out of mine; it comes out of the pockets of all the taxpayers. It is computed on the same income tax form upon which we make out our tax return. It is forwarded to the same income tax office; and the security tax payment itself is made with the same cheque and with the same kind of money, as is suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood. Usually it is borrowed money; we have to negotiate loans from the bank to pay it. How anyone can distinguish between them and say it is not included in 68108-1614
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan the computation of the tax is something beyond my understanding. In any event, as has been pointed out by others who have preceded me in the debate, the extent of the relief is such that the vast majority of the people do not benefit by the reduction at all.
I was looking up the statistics prepared by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) as they apply to my own constituency. I find that in the county of Annapolis there are 21,747 people, and that of that number 920 pay income tax. In the county of Kings there are 33,183 people of whom 2,100 pay income tax. We realize that they are the heads of families. In some cases there may be two or three children who would benefit directly or indirectly from this reduction. But when you take that proportion and see how low it is when compared with the vast majority of people in these constituencies-and this would apply to every constituency across Canada-then one must suggest that the relief obtained from the budget does not warrant the pounding of the heavy bass drum of propaganda which was beating so long and so loudly after the budget was brought down, and which apparently had been all set up for playing many, many days before the budget was delivered.
Hon. members on this side of the house on more than one occasion have suggested a reduction in the sales tax. We have pointed out many times that there is no tax which could be reduced with less impact upon the treasury and greater impact upon the taxpayer than this particular one. I shall not repeat the arguments which have been made already, but we know how the pyramiding takes place in the hands of the wholesaler, in the hands of the broker and then in the hands of the retailer. The proportion of that tax borne by the consumer is out of all proportion to the amount the treasury receives, in its original application.
There could be a reduction made in the sales tax which would be beneficial to all the taxpayers, and which would not cost the treasury a tremendous amount. Of course we realize that this is an indirect or a hidden tax, and I suppose the political kudos for having done away with it would not be such as to permit the minister to pose as a Santa Claus.
In the second place, the budget is criticized because it is superficial and is not based upon savings or economies of any kind. That was dealt with most ably this morning in an editorial appearing in the Montreal Gazette, where it is pointed out that the minister has referred to the budget as a social dividend. The editorial goes on to suggest that if it
2530	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan is a social dividend, then surely it is something payable to society as a whole. Yet we see from his own figures and from estimates before us that more money is to be taken from society as a whole, and that the taxpayers as a whole are made the losers. If that is so, how one can term it a social dividend is more than I can understand. And, as the Gazette suggests, it is at the best a discounted one.
You have to anticipate the fact that inflation will not wreck the financial structure, and anticipate the fact that the gross national product will continue to increase, and anticipate the fact that expenditures will be held at a level which has been suggested. That is quite a stretch of the imagination, when one considers what is done by -this government.
You have to imagine all those things; and then you are faced with the fact that, at the end, more money will be taken out of the group as a whole than was- taken last year, because no economies are being made, no greater savings being made, than were made before.
As an aside, let me say that I listened to the hon. member who preceded me in the debate read from an editorial in the Globe and Mail; and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) on Friday afternoon dealt at length with certain alleged statements he said were made with respect to family allowances. The inference was obvious, that when we talk about economies we are talking about economies which can be made in the field of social security. Well, I trust that record has been played for the last time by hon. members opposite.
