speechtext:
It may have been good music, but it sounded muted and did not make the impression it would have made at one time. I was going to say that there seems to be an attempt at this time to develop such a record with respect to social security, and that it


would be in the same category as the kind of musical program the C.B.C. was playing on Sunday afternoons.
Without further elaboration of the facts, we do know that economies can be made; and they can be made without interfering in any way with one cent of expenditure for social security in this country. That is what the people have been asking for, economy and savings. That is what they have not been getting from this government, and certainly did not get from the budget.
I am reminded of what happened in France in the early days, when Marie Antoinette said, "Let them eat cake", when the people were asking for bread. Well, in this budget we did not even get our cake; we got only a little frosting. Indeed, I think we were offered a macaroon, rather than a cake, on this occasion.
I do not think many of the smaller people of this country have as great an appreciation of these alleged reductions as they would have if they received a little better treatment from those responsible for collecting taxes. I am not in position to speak as to the inner workings of the Department of National Revenue, but certain things are obvious. They tell us that they have caught up with their arrears. We know they have a large staff to do this.
But we find now that there is a large staff out in the country driving around from place to place and making surveys as to arrears of taxation on the part of farmers and small businessmen who filed their returns years ago. As far as they knew these people felt that those returns had been complete and had been accepted. Then along come this group of collectors looking for taxpayers in the same way a fisherman looks for trout in a pool. When they find a prosperous farmhouse they go in and start giving the farmer the works.
I know in my county they were driving along the other day and they saw a farmhouse with a new chimney and fireplace. They decided that if this man could afford to build a fireplace they had better put him through the wringer. So they went in and started to work on him. Before they got through they had built up a net worth statement going back into the 1930's and coming down into the 1940's almost to the present time. They alleged that they had found that in 1942 he must have taken in a little more money than he reported because he had installed a monel metal sink so that his wife would not have to wash the dishes in the old wooden sink. They assessed him for arrears of income tax in that year. Of course

they say to these people, "If we are wrong you can go to the exchequer court and fight it out; if you can prove we are wrong, we will withdraw the assessment". That is a sample of the treatment handed out.
These farmers and small businessmen are expected to keep the type of records which the United States Steel Corporation does not keep, and which certainly the Department of National Defence does not keep. If they cannot produce that kind of records they are assessed.
You would think that when they had dealt once with a man they would leave him alone, but there is a farmer in my county who was assessed for $700 tax in a certain year, let us say 1942. He went to a lawyer and told him that he had no records and could not remember anything about that year. In checking through some old material he found that in that year he had cashed a life insurance policy which accounted for the increase in his bank account, and wiped out the tax for which he was assessed.
One would have thought that that would have been the end of it; but no, not at all. Having beaten them on that, or having satisfied them that he had a reasonable explanation which they had always denied, they came along six months later and made another net worth assessment in which they took in another year or two years. They assessed him for about $800 for that year. After making inquiries it developed that in that year he had married the second time and his wife, who had been a widow, had sold her farm and equipment and had deposited the proceeds in his bank account. That wiped out the second assessment.
What happened then? They waited another six months. I do not know how many men were reviewing this man's file, but they were determined to get him some way. So they assessed him for about $1,600 for another year, overlooking the previous assessments which had been made.
I had a man come into my office not long ago to tell me that two or three years ago he had retired from his farm and was in receipt of an old age pension. He had turned his farm over to his son. He had filed income tax returns for each year he had been in operation. He went to the department and asked them if there was any further information he could give them. They assured him that everything was quite clear, that he had filed his returns properly and there was nothing more he needed to do about it. Three months ago he was assessed for arrears of income tax, made up largely of interest, amounting to $1,800.
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan
This is typical of what is happening in this country. I believe it is happening in every province, and it is certainly going on in the rural areas of Nova Scotia. I cannot see any excuse for a department as well manned and as efficiently run as this department, having all the complicated accounting machinery that is available, and having everything in the form of records of all taxpayers, waiting for years and years and then coming along and reviewing the assessments of these individuals who are completely honest.
I am not saying a word for the man who has not filed a return or who has cooked up his return. I am not saying a word on behalf of the business which conceals income, which is simply fraud. But when two or three years have elapsed an assessment should not be open for review and these men who are honest should not be penalized or charged interest which quite often is more than the original tax.
These reductions in income tax have done nothing to ease the plight of many taxpayers across the country. There was a time when the government was not as omnipotent or omniscient as it professes to be now. It is hard to believe it, but after the war this government indicated that it felt there was going to be a depression, and attempted to prepare for it. They had a shelf of public works and many other things. They were so anxious to avoid excess unemployment that they decided to send home all married women who were in government employ or m the employ of industry. Certain tax reductions which had been in existence were revoked.
Instead of a depression we now have full employment, inflation and a high cost of living, due largely to government policies adopted at that time when there was fear of a depression. We are faced with a bad housing situation across this country. Many young married couples are finding it hard to get established. We hear talk of revising mortgage arrangements in an effort to encourage the building of houses and the establishment of homes by young people. But how can they do this with the present high cost of living and the burdens which they have to carry?
I suggest that if the minister had wanted to help a large group in this country which needs help, the many thousands of young married couples from Halifax to Vancouver, from St. John's to Victoria, where the wife has to work in order to help meet the cost of living and the responsibilities of establishing a home, he should see that these people are not penalized by the provisions of the
2532	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan Income Tax Act which puts them on a different basis than that of other married couples.
There is a large group of young people in this country-many of us have them in our own families-young men and women who are trying to establish homes for themselves but who are penalized by the cost of living and the inflationary policies of this government. They are finding it most difficult to carry on. I suggest that if the minister had wanted to be of assistance to a fairly large group something should have been done that would have been of more assistance than perhaps some of the other things which have been done.
I see my time is running out, and there are many phases of this matter with which I should like to deal. I think I have about seven or eight minutes left, or perhaps ten minutes.
I was intrigued the other day by the speech made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley), who is not in the house at the moment. He dealt with certain phases of the problems of the maritimes when he was discussing the budget. Altogether he painted a very doleful tale with which 1 certainly am not fully in accord. I think he said that our industries could not stand competition. I do not accept that in full. The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) can think of an industry in his constituency which is in competition with others all across Canada in that particular line. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Stanfield) is associated with an industry that is in competition with others across the country. The hon. members for Halifax have industries in their riding which are in competition across Canada. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George) has a heavy steel industry at Sackville making furnaces and stoves which is competing successfully with other similar industries across Canada.
In saying that, I do not want to minimize for a moment the difficult economic circumstances in which industries in the maritimes generally find themselves, but I do not accept for one minute the statement that there are many industries down there which find it impossible to stand competition. Nor do I like the suggestion that if it were not for the moneys being received from mothers' allowances, old age pensions and other matters-I think his implication was obvious-we would be getting no money in the maritimes at all. Whether or not the hon. member meant it, that was certainly the implication he left. Personally I did not like it, and it is untrue. We are not people who are supplicants. We are not asking for largesse from the federal treasury.


Given the opportunity we can earn our own living in that area, as we have in the past, equally with people in the rest of Canada.
But I do agree with him that there are economic difficulties. There are difficulties with respect to freight rates and also other problems which need attention. He referred to certain remarks of mine which he said I had made some time ago, but he did not mention that at that time I raised the question of the movement of freight through Canadian ports and pointed out that during the past few years there has been a marked reduction in the export of Canadian goods through eastern Canadian ports. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) spoke the other day he referred to the great increase in our trade with Latin America, an increase from approximately $40 million to over $500 million. I wonder through what ports that trade is proceeding. Certainly it is not going through the ports of the eastern seaboard.
We in the opposition should be complimented by the suggestion of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert that after all it was our responsibility and we should do something about it. I realize that we will have additional responsibilities in the not too distant future and probably will have to deal with it at that time. It was a tribute to the opposition.
The hon. member said he has had a heavy heart during the past winter over the situation. I thought he looked his usual debonair self; and when he did not, I thought he was probably worrying about the action of the government with respect to the port of Saint John, because it is the responsibility of the government if action has to be taken in these matters.
I do not think one accomplishes much in this field by making sarcastic references to big businessmen, wealthy interests or anything of that kind. After all, whatever may have been the influence of wealthy businessmen in the past on any political party, certainly anyone who knows the workings of government in Canada today, with a centralized government such as we have-I am not saying this politically; it may be necessary-knows that in this country the minister of trade and commerce, the minister of finance and the minister of defence production exercise more influence on industry with their little fingers than do all the financial colonels so-called to whom reference has occasionally been made in the past.
Let us not hear any more talk about the influence of wealthy men or what they can do to assist in solving these problems. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert said that

leadership was needed now, and I agree with him. That is what we have been saying. We have said that there has been a lack of vision, and we are glad to hear these criticisms coming from the government side although it is a rather belated repentance. Saul of Tarsus saw a great light when he was on the way down to Damascus, and he kicked against the pricks. Apparently my hon. friend also saw a great light when he suggested there was a lack of leadership and a lack of vision. I am glad to hear his voice raised in this connection in support of those who have spoken about it from this side of the house, and I am looking forward to the time when more leadership will come from that side of the house than there is at the moment.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) spoke a moment ago. I am not going to deal at length with his department now because his estimates will be before the house and we can deal with them at a later date. Anyone who knows the situation on the east coast will agree that more fish have been caught this year than ever before. The warehouses and storage plants are full of fish. The market price has broken, and there is a marketing problem which must be faced. The Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to Cuba the other day, and the great development in the market there for maritime products. It is true that we are selling in Cuba a certain amount of salt, cured and smoked fish. That amount has been constant for some years. But something must and should be done to encourage the development of our own Canadian market for fish.
It is all right to talk about the development of South American markets. We welcome it. It is all right to talk about the importance of the United States market. We appreciate these markets and realize that we must maintain our connections, but far less fish is consumed in Canada than in almost any other nation in the world. There could be encouragement, impetus and leadership given there which is lacking today, and to that one looks with some degree of anticipation for the future.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) spoke very forcibly the other day about the coal and steel industry of the mari-times and the plight in which it finds itself. I am not associating myself with him in all the things he said about the operations there, but I do agree with him that it is one of the primary industries upon which the maritime economy, and particularly the Nova Scotian economy, is dependent. The other two are agriculture and fishing.
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
What does the budget have for the agriculturist? Nothing at all. Figures have been given in the house about the decline in agricultural production over the last few years. Last Friday the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) spoke forcibly on that point. There has been a reduction of 13 per cent in farmers' income and an increase in their labour costs and other costs of production. If that is the average reduction across Canada, as it is, it is far greater in the east. You can say what you like about the beauties of trade moving north and south-and we accept that as far as you can develop it-but the fact remains that we have been brought up and are dependent upon an economy which necessitates substantial trade moving east and west across the Atlantic to Great Britain and other sterling markets.
We read that Great Britain is facing a deficiency in trade and that some adjustments must be made in that connection but certainly there is no suggestion of encouragement in that regard so far as the budget is concerned. The apple producers and potato growers and farmers generally of my constituency have to get more extended markets than they have today. So far as the fruit growing industry is concerned, it is true that last year we had a small crop and therefore were not faced with the disastrous circumstances that ordinarily would prevail, but in the coming year we hope to have an average crop and if so it is absolutely essential to get access to the sterling markets. Otherwise we will face a really serious situation indeed.
There are other matters with which one could deal. While the minister is here I should have liked to refer to educational grants, but we will probably have a chance to deal with that subject when his estimates are before the house. It is a matter of substantial importance to the maritimes and the universities of the east, and it must be discussed. However, I do not want to trespass beyond my time, and I shall leave those observations until later.

On page 2121 of Hansard, in his budget speech, he said:
The government has not relaxed its efforts toward maximum economy and efficiency in all government operations.
That is the same old assurance he has been giving us year in and year out. What are the facts? When you examine page 82 of the budget papers you find that in the current fiscal year spending is up in all but two departments-those of the Secretary of State and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In the case of the former the reduction was very minor. The reduction in the case of the Department of Trade and Commerce was more substantial, but the reason was not because of economies. In 1951 we had a census and in 1952 we did not.
During the past year civilian expenditures, or non-defence expenditures, have been more than $100 million greater than in the previous year. If there is any evidence of economy there I wish some Liberal member would tell me where it is. The fact is that the economy drive which the government announced some years ago has pretty well broken down. This government has discounted and disparaged any suggestions for savings which have been made in the house, and it does not seem to be very much interested in economy. In parliamentary circles the word "economy" sounds like a foreign language. The Liberals say in effect: We are living in dangerous times. Defence spending and social service spending are high. We are caught on the wheel of fate, and nothing can be done.
I do not believe that thinking of this kind should exist in a dynamic country like Canada. I say that cuts in federal expenditures are possible, desirable and feasible. Large sums could be saved, I suggest, by the introduction of sound business methods into government. Parliament, in running the biggest business in the country, frequently adopts methods and practices which would quickly bankrupt any small business. I mention again, as I have many times in the past, the duplication of services in this building. About thirty odd departments are completely duplicated. What business would not do something about such a situation, particularly after it was pointed out?
I still cannot understand why the government does not adopt central purchasing. I doubt if there is a single large company in Canada which does not have a central purchasing department. They have to have, if they are going to buy efficiently. However, here in Ottawa instead of central buying we have dozens of departments and agencies,

each one spending vast sums of money for the crown. We have even had cases of one department bidding against another. I think this is something to which the government should give attention.
I wonder how often private business would use the cost-plus method of letting construction contracts. In this past year a high percentage of the construction contracts awarded by the Department of National Defence was on a cost-plus basis. I contend that the practice has cost the Canadian taxpayers many millions of extra dollars.
I heard a story last week which, in my opinion, sums up the weakness of this cost-plus method of giving contracts. Two salesmen who were interested in getting defence contracts came to Ottawa from the city of Toronto. They worked all day and decided, after five o'clock, that they would like to have a round of drinks. So they went down to the Chateau Laurier, to the Jasper room, and sat down at a table. The first salesman said "Let me buy this round of drinks. I am on an expense account." The second said: "No, let me buy the round, my company has a cost-plus contract with the government, and we might as well make a profit on the round."
That, I think, sums up the weakness of these cost-plus contracts. Government officials in the past have themselves admitted the weakness. Yet, despite such an admission, if you look at the public accounts, for this year, pages N-23 to N-65, you will find that in the last fiscal year the Department of National Defence alone let 231 contracts on a cost-plus basis, valued at well over S106 million. Small wonder that our defence is costing us so heavily.
Perhaps there may have been some reason for cost-plus contracts in the war emergency, but I say there is no excuse whatever for them today. I think the government could save the taxpayers a good deal of money if, in the future, all contracts were let on a tender basis.
Today about half our budget is being spent for national defence. It is quite true that taxation adequate to build up our defences at home, and carry out our commitments abroad, has been approved by all parties in this house, and I am sure that support will continue. However, after several years of rearming, a great many Canadians are alarmed to find that in order to equip one man in the armed forces of the United Kingdom it costs $5,000, in order to do the same in the United States it costs about $13,000, but here in Canada it costs $18,000 to $20,000. It is very difficult to understand 68108-162
The Bridget-Mr. Thatcher why our defence costs should be so out of line with those in Britain and in the United States.
In this debate I am not permitted to discuss the Currie report. However, I want to say that on every hand there is increasing evidence of neglect and carelessness in the administration of the armed forces. It is now fairly clear that the government has tossed money around recklessly on defence in the past year.

I do not think it is so reckless. I charge this government with milking the Canadian taxpayer in those years to provide frills in defence spending. I read a news item which Arthur Blakely of the Montreal Gazette wrote for his newspaper about a week ago, on defence expenditures. I thought it was an effective job, and very well done. I refer hon. members for a moment to the public accounts of last year, pages N-35 to N-60. You will find some pretty interesting reading if you look there.
In the first place, as has been pointed out in recent days, you will find 25 contracts for landscaping various government buildings, with more than a million dollars spent for this particular service. At Fort Nelson, $27,500 was paid out for the construction of a single well. At Wainwright, Alberta, a swimming pool cost $22,000; a gymnasium, $280,000; bowling alleys, $54,000. Is it for such things that this government is taxing the Canadian people? On page N-32 of the public accounts we find that to provide the Wainwright army camp with water, it cost $1,830,000. This figure seems to be rather excessive.
Here in Ottawa, at No. 26 central ordnance depot, over $25,000 was spent on air conditioning offices. At Longue Pointe a ventilating system for one building cost the taxpayers $48,000. At Whitehorse in the Yukon, according to page N-35 of the public accounts, the government spent $701,000 to erect 30 prefabricated houses. This works out at a cost of $23,380 per house. I know that transportation costs are quite high, but that figure certainly seems excessive to me. At Churchill the department paid $7,765 to an architect simply to design a chapel and I can find no evidence that the design was ever used.
Now, despite the fact that we have a good many architects on the federal payroll, several millions of dollars were paid in fees during the last fiscal year for architectural services. On page N-24 of the public accounts we see that 500 huts were built at Bouchard,
2536	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher Quebec, at a cost of $3,555,000. This works out to $7,110 each, and these were huts, not houses. On page N-35, we And that another 500 were built by Eastern Woodworkers Limited, at a cost of $4,343,000 or $8,700 each. These huts were not used, but were placed in storage at a military camp at De-bert. On page N-36, we find 140 more of these huts which were built by North American Buildings Limited at a cost of $1,177,000. This works out to $8,400 each. These huts are stored in Edmonton. I doubt whether, in such expenditures, the taxpayer is receiving value for his dollar.
At Dartmouth one street in the married quarters area cost $100,000. At page N-38 we find that engineering services incidental to the design of a heating installation cost the taxpayer $31,560. On page N-39 we find that it cost $110,000 to rough grade streets and lanes in the married quarters of Belmont park. The paving of streets and driveways in the same area cost another $144,000. Across Canada millions of dollars were spent in these camps to pave streets, sidewalks, parking lots and parade squares.
On page N-41 we find that $314,000 was paid at Greenwood to replace sub-floors in various R.C.A.F. buildings. At St. Hubert $15,000 was paid for inspection of various runways. At St. Hubert also $38,500 was spent for a five-cell guardhouse. Construction of a single mess at Camp Borden cost $560,000. At Centralia, according to page N-48, renovating and partitioning a barracks cost $475,000. Repairs to hangar aprons, taxi strips and parking areas cost $57,000. On page N-61, we find that a lean-to at Fort Nelson cost $36,000. Alterations and additions to the officers' mess at Kingston cost the taxpayer $340,000. In Quebec an armoury was re-wired and re-lighted at a cost of $67,000, while one in Sherbrooke cost $30,500.
I say that on every hand, Mr. Speaker, there is evidence of extravagant spending and lax administration in the armed services. Thieving is apparently much more widespread than Canadians realize. From June 1, 1950 to November 24, 1952, there were 601 fires at defence establishments, causing damage of over $5 million. There are many indications that a number of these fires were deliberately set in order to hide shortages of equipment and stock. I quote from a report in the Ottawa Journal:
Second most costly fire in Canada's defence establishments in the two-and-a-half-year period was that at No. 26 ordnance depot, Flouffe Park,


Ottawa. Losses in that blaze are placed at $673,832, and cause of the fire is listed as "suspected arson".
Two outbreaks of fire at Petawawa military camp causing losses of $188,096 are also set down to suspected arson. In a fire at Winnipeg in which property to the value of $12,000, the cause is definitely cited as "arson".
I do not think I have to tell hon. members that it looks as if something is wrong, when such situations can arise.
In my opinion, there is another way this government is spending money needlessly at the present time on defence. I seriously question the wisdom of this country spending many millions of dollars pioneering in the field of military weapons. It seems to me that this phase of defence could be more economically and more efficiently undertaken by the larger allied nations who are better equipped for the purpose. To give one example, Canada at the moment is spending hundreds of millions of dollars pioneering in the field of advanced military aviation. Every hon. member knows that much of that work is being duplicated by other NATO countries.
This government spent millions of dollars subsidizing the Avro company in building a jet transport plane. One plane came off the assembly line, and the project was dropped because it was found that the British Comet had a cruising range almost three times as great as the Avro plane. I believe also that it is fairly apparent to an unbiased observer that the CF-100 project, if it is not a fiasco, is at least a very very costly experiment. For four years now this project has dawdled along and has cost the taxpayer well over $100 million, according to the last figures I saw. I understand that so far 16 planes have been delivered from the assembly line. Even if that project is not a dud, unless something is done to get quantity production soon, I think there is a real danger that the plane may be obsolete.
It is very interesting to note that around the same time the government embarked on the F-86 Sabre project. I understand that, in the same period, roughly 700 of those planes have been turned out. Although it may give us a sense of pride to read of Canadian achievement in this field, at the same time we should keep in mind the staggering costs which are involved in such experimentation. In addition to the cost there is always the danger of the new weapons bogging down some place between the blueprint stage and the production line. I contend that the taxpayers would save millions of dollars annually and have weapons which are just as good or better, if in the future the government left most of the design

headaches to Britain and the United States. After all, they have better facilities for this work. Canadian manufacturers could concentrate on the best American and British weapons under some licence arrangement.
Everyone wants Canada to have adequate defence, but more and more Canadians are asking themselves whether they are better defended because the defence department goes on periodical wild buying streaks; because the defence department decides to build swimming pools and bowling alleys; because it decides to fix up officers' messes in a very plush way, because it beautifully landscapes defence projects. The evidence is mounting daily that the government's own officials have warned them in the past that there is something wrong in the department of defence. Yet those reports apparently have been ignored. Apparently a special government investigator, in September, 1949, made a damning report to the government, according to evidence which was brought forward last week. According to the Montreal Gazette of February 26, it contained sentences like these:
I could not fail to be impressed with the fact that for such a tremendous administrative machine, there appears to be little effective fighting strength.
And another one:
A tremendous amount of money is being spent to provide an administrative machine which, to my way of thinking, occupies a large part of its time in a futile paper war with the reserve army which has neither the strength in numbers, the equipment, nor the inclination to respond.
There were other sentences. I repeat that this is a damning report, and I am amazed that the government refused even to discuss it. In view of evidence like that, how can any Liberal say that the average taxpayer is receiving value for his defence dollar? Despite all of these reports, the government continues to increase defence spending. All parties in this house, and most citizens in the country have in the past backed government demands for adequate defence appropriations; but many citizens of the country are beginning to doubt whether those appropriations have been well spent. Personally I sincerely believe that defence costs could be cut not by 10 per cent but by 15 per cent or 20 per cent if the government really got down to business.
I say this budget has failed to meet the main financial problem facing the Canadian people, namely the need to reduce federal expenditures. At a time when tax relief is urgently needed, this Liberal government continues on a spending spree which is unparalleled in our history. A few months ago a United States government was overturned. One of the reasons it was overturned was the 68108-162^
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher corruption, waste and inefficiency which had crept into the administration. It is becoming daily more apparent that Canadians will be forced to take similar action if they want to get taxes back to a reasonable level. This government is tired. It has been too long in office. It is encumbered by deadwood and hangers on; and it lacks the initiative needed to meet the challenge of overtaxation. I say that federal waste and extravagance have reached scandalous proportions in this country. In view of that fact, I think the only honourable course for this government to take is to resign without delay. By that I mean to resign, not next August or September, but this week. I challenge the Liberal party to go to the people with this budget as an issue. I say that the people of Canada will welcome the opportunity to show their dissatisfaction at the polls.

subtopic: TERMINATION OF ABNORMAL SITUATION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The President of the United States today proclaimed the termination of the abnormal situation in respect of cattle and meats which has been in effect in the United States since 1943. During the existence of the abnormal situation all tariff quota arrangements on cattle were suspended.
As a result of this announcement the tariff arrangements on cattle negotiated at Geneva in 1947 will apply from April 1. The Geneva agreement provided for increases in the annual tariff quotas from 225,000 to 400,000 head of heavyweight cattle weighing 700 pounds and over, and from 125,000 to 200,000 head for calves. Quarterly quotas within the annual quota of 400,000 head of heavyweight cattle were increased from 60,000 head to 120,000 head per quarter. A lower rate of duty of 1J cents per pound applies on imports within the tariff quota for calves and heavyweight cattle. Cattle and calves imported into the United States in excess of the quotas are dutiable at 2 J cents per pound. Dairy cows enter at 1J cents per pound and purebred cattle for the improvement of stock are admitted free, without tariff quota limitations in either case.

I should like to address you, Mr. Speaker, on the point of order raised by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet prior to the dinner adjournment and continued by him now with the argument which he has just delivered.
The facts pertaining to the case in question are, I understand, the following: An appeal was taken to the income tax appeal board by a certain Quebec corporation, against an assessment made by the Department of National Revenue in relation to its taxable income, the point involving the right of the company to claim deduction on account of certain school rates paid in the province of Quebec.
The income tax appeal board upheld the appeal and found that the assessment had not been correctly made. From that decision of the income tax appeal board an appeal was taken by the Minister of National Revenue to the exchequer court. The appeal to the exchequer court was sustained, and the decision was handed down just a few days ago.
There, Mr. Speaker, according to my information the matter rests. No further appeal has been taken yet. An appeal might be taken later; there is still time for an


appeal. An appeal will not be open to the Minister of National Revenue; it will be an appeal open to the corporation in question, but as yet the fact is that no appeal has been taken.
That, in my submission to you, Mr. Speaker, is conclusive of the point raised by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage). Had an appeal been taken and were that appeal now pending he would be quite right in his contention that the matter is sub judice, but as no appeal is pending at the present time and as none has been taken the matter is not sub judice; therefore, it is perfectly competent for any member of this house to discuss the subject matter of the decision, whether of the income tax appeal board or of the exchequer court.
As my hon. friend has said, the reference is to paragraph 246 (c) of Beauchesne's third edition, where we find the following:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 41, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:
And then paragraph (c):
refer to any matter on which a judicial decision is pending;
Will you please observe, Mr. Speaker, the words "any matter on which a judicial decision is pending". That is to say, in my submission, a matter in which some proceeding has been taken to the court upon which the court has not yet delivered a decision. The only other two references in Beauchesne are, as I have no doubt you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, paragraphs 252 and 490, neither of which I think is of direct assistance to us on this point.
But my hon. friend the member for Montmagny-L'Islet has quoted May, fifteenth edition and has invoked the expression "matters awaiting the adjudication of a court of law". On that phrase the hon. member bases an argument that until a matter is disposed of conclusively by the final court of law that matter is sub judice; and if the time for entering an appeal has not fully run, the matter is still sub judice.
In my submission, Mr. Speaker, that would be a most unwarrantable extension of the rule. There is nothing pending in the courts about this case at the moment. It may be that at some later time, perhaps a month from now, the matter will come back to the courts if notice of appeal is served on the minister by the corporation in question, but at the present time there is no proceeding pending before the courts. The income tax appeal board is through with it, and the exchequer court is through with it. There is nothing pending before the Supreme Court of Canada

at this moment, and that is the only court to which an appeal can be taken from the exchequer court.
Therefore, at this moment, there is nothing pending before any court. There is no proceeding before any court in this land on this matter that is awaiting judicial decision. No judicial decision is pending within the rule as stated in Beauchesne, paragraph 246 (c). In my submission, Mr. Speaker, the point taken by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet is not well taken, and my colleague the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) is perfectly within his rights in proceeding to discuss a matter which, so far as the exchequer court is concerned, is disposed of now, so far as the income tax appeal board is concerned is disposed of now, and is not pending before any court in the country.

I submit that we should accept this judicial interpretation of "pendente lite"; and there is no suit before the court until notice of appeal has been given. There is no litigation. Nothing has been done to weaken the force of another rule of a similar kind, that no reference must be made in debate to matters before the courts of law in some pending litigation.

speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker. When the house took recess at ten minutes to six I wanted to draw its attention to the section of the Income Tax Act to which the federal government resorts to levy a tax on contributions made by certain taxpayers of Quebec, corporations and individuals, to the special education fund set up by the Quebec provincial government.
I would like to give a brief outline of the creation of this fund.
In 1946, school boards, large and small, were in terrible financial straits. A large number of them were more or less bankrupt. Not only were they unable to borrow but they could not even amortize their debt or even pay the interest.
Most of the school boards were physically incapable of improving their schools and even less of constructing new ones. Due to our traditionally large families, classes were soon overcrowded. Notwithstanding the good intentions of the school trustees and of the government, teachers were receiving starvation wages because it was impossible to tax real property any more. The position was tragic. Our whole system of primary education was paralysed.
It was then that the provincial government decided to create a special fund in order to assume all the debts of all the school boards.
Finally the primary schools in our towns and in the country as well, the very basis of our system of education, were going to be salvaged and put on a progressive basis and would afford to give the French-Canadian youth of the province of Quebec the training essential to their future.
These huge liabilities had reached the fantastic figure of $100 million. The provincial government decided to use the resources of the province to build up this educational fund.
The government called upon all those who owned hydraulic resources and those who developed the huge forestry resources of the province of Quebec, beyond the boundaries of the school municipalities.
Thus, a tax of 15 cents per cord was levied on all the lumber cut on the crown lands and of 10 cents per thousand kilowatt hours with regard to all the power developments located on crown lands or held by right of

property. Later on, the oil and the telephone companies were also required to do their share.
But although these contributions had been used exclusively for the purposes of the fund, that is to help education, the federal income tax department refused to consider this contribution as a school tax and it taxed these amounts as being part of the profits of the said companies and individuals.
Yet, these contributions, paid for a legitimate purpose by all the companies operating in the province of Quebec, represent in fact necessary operating expenses for all those who wish to operate lumbering enterprises or hydroelectric works. Besides, the income tax law aims at taxing profits and not expenses.
But, by some stretch of the imagination, the dominion puts those expenses in the category of corporation taxes-even in such cases when it is possible to deduct from this contribution the school taxes which companies or private citizens pay to the various school boards where those companies own properties.
Moreover, from the constitutional standpoint, the thing is quite clear: those taxes are nothing but school taxes-paid in order to provide for the educational needs within the province of Quebec.
By taxing this fund, the federal government would set the first example since 1917 of school taxes which might not be deducted from the income tax. By following such a policy the income tax department would discriminate against the Quebec corporations, as Quebec would thus become the only province where school taxes would not be deducted from the income tax.
Confronted with this attitude adopted by income tax officers, some electricity companies decided to protest against this encroachment of the federal government, by appealing to the income tax appeal board; strangely enough, this board, set up by the dominion itself, has refused to acknowledge the claims of the national revenue department and has delivered a circumstantial judgment.
Logically, this decision should have satisfied the federal government, had they been so scrupulously intent on preserving the rights of the provinces. Had they truly intended to recognize as an exclusive preserve of these governments the field of education and the direct taxes to be levied for that sole purpose, they were there provided with a wonderful opportunity of showing the people that they meant to leave the provinces free to levy those school taxes which they might require.
The Budget-Mr. Balcer
At that time, in order to do away with any possible confusion they could have clarified their own regulations or amended the Income Tax Act so that, according to the spirit of confederation, the holders of water power in Quebec would not be taxed twice for having assisted the Quebec primary schools. Such, however, is not the case. The very same people who are at present attempting to blackmail Quebec with their grants to universities, decided to appeal the decision of their own court to the Exchequer Court of Canada.	|l
And there, unfortunately, their appeal was sustained, but not before the judge had expressed the opinion that he is bound by the orders in council and that even though, from any logical business point of view it would seem that these taxes should be deductible, it was his duty to enforce the law as expressed by parliament.
I sincerely believe, Mr. Speaker, that there is a case which demonstrates the necessity of holding a federal-provincial conference in order to define once and for all, if not in an equitable fashion, the taxation fields that belong to the central government. After all, in this case the government is actually taxing twice those companies who have had to make certain outlays in order to contribute to the establishment of a fund to help education in one province.
The fact that the federal government refuses to consider as a school tax a contribution to such a fund and denies these companies the right to deduct these expenses which for them are compulsory, puts these companies in an inferior position in regard to companies paying school taxes in the other provinces.
Besides, the fathers of confederation wished without any doubt, to reserve to the provincial legislatures, under section 93, the exclusive right of legislation in matters of education. And this exclusive right which is guaranteed by section 93 would become an illusory right if another exclusive right were attached to it, that is the one under section 92, which provides for legislation on direct taxation in the province in order to levy funds for provincial purposes.
If the provincial legislature has the exclusive right of legislation with regard to the levying of the necessary funds for education purposes, it is unconstitutional for the federal government to impose a new tax on these school taxes which are paid for the sole purpose of aiding education.
2546	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Balcer
These taxes which are being levied by the federal government amount to over $2 million a year. Might it be, then, that the $2 million for the universities which the federal government wants the province of Quebec to accept and is so insistent upon it, is the same $2 million which is being levied on the contributions to our elementary schools? If such is the case, one must admit that the formula is rather lacking in elegance. In other words, $2 million is being taken away from the companies which help elementary schools and this money is being used as gifts to universities.
The federal government accumulates surpluses and is in a position to blackmail the Quebec government with grants to universities or with direct subsidies in the amount of $50 million, in return for taxation rights. The federal government is satisfied to place Quebec in a position where it has the choice between $50 million or agreeing to surrender forever vested rights. The Quebec government shows quite a strong will in refusing the $50 million because it well realizes that part of those $50 million comes from taxes collected in the province and that there are many fields of administration where the money could be well spent.
But we all know that if Quebec refuses those direct subsidies it is to check Ottawa's centralizing efforts.
The federal government boasts of assisting in the building of hospitals, of paying old age pensions, family allowances, and granting moneys for the construction of highways. All these fields are allocated to the provinces by the constitution but the federal government has encroached upon them. If you let the federal government take over one right, you soon find that it never gives it back.
The federal government always seems to have too much money and always wants to make gifts, but it never returns to the provinces taxation fields they claim as theirs.
Yet sections 92 and 93 of the constitution state that education, hospitals, highways and social services come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
Why should the central government interfere in those fields? The main reason is that it is the only one in a position to offer such gifts. Now that it has those sources of taxation which it took over during the two wars, it has the upper hand in so far as taxation in our country is concerned.
Where the federal government has passed, there is nothing left for either the provinces or the municipalities.
[Mr. Balcer.1

What substantial social service improvements would the provinces not grant, if they could do so by reasonably taxing the taxpayers. For let us not forget that whatever be the source of taxation-municipal, provincial or federal-it is always the same taxpayer who pays.
And we see today municipalities on the verge of bankruptcy, confronted with well-founded requests for municipal services and unable to meet them.
In their turn, they look to the provinces for assistance, since property taxes can no longer suffice while the other taxation sources have been drained by the federal government.
But the federal government, rather than giving back the least of those taxation fields which they took over during the wars, prefer encroaching upon those fields that do not concern them.
Our whole federative system is being jeopardized. Every day the federal authority takes a further step in the same direction. Though the Minister of Finance asserts with a pious and offended look that the present government has no centralizing tendencies, the encroachments of his government upon fields which do not concern them prove just the opposite.
We have now come to a point where any objection to federal interference in fields strictly provincial brings immediate cries of separatism and isolationism from the central government's followers.
When the premier of Quebec insists on having the fields of taxation objectively defined instead of accepting the gifts and intervention of the federal government, there are cries that "he stoops to mean politics". Should he refuse to heed to blackmailing under the guise of federal grants to universities, it is said that he seeks to destroy Canadian unity.
It is the duty of all provincial governments to claim the fields of taxation they need for the administration of their respective provinces. But the government of the province of Quebec has yet another reason to be very careful and jealous of its rights. It is not by accident that we have a federal system instead of a Unitarian state.
Ours is a federal state because there happened to be two different racial groups in Canada when confederation took place; in Lower Canada lived a group of the French Canadian race.
In 1867, the leaders of the French Canadians played the part that French-Canadian history had wrought for them.

French-speaking Canadians had seen their racial group recognized and their rights enlarged first under a responsible government and finally along with all our democratic freedoms.
Since confederation and thanks to confederation, the whole of Canada has developed at an extraordinary pace and has become one of the foremost industrial powers of the world.
Its population has risen to almost fifteen million people, nearly one-third being French-Canadian.
Canada is an example of two racial groups living side by side in the best of spirit. But the French-speaking group is still very jealous of its rights whilst remaining fundamentally Canadian.
It is therefore deeply regrettable to see the spirit of the constitution of 1867 deteriorating constantly through the actions of the federal government and it is also deeply regrettable to see the province of Quebec isolated from the other provinces and, for the first time since confederation, in a position of inferiority.
Quebec is accused of separatism if it refuses to sign agreements which restrict the powers and the rights of provincial governments. It is suggested that Quebec wants to live alone and become a part of the country in which French Canadians would be isolated. But Quebec has always shown tolerance and worked for Canadian unity. In no other province is to be found, in the field of education for instance, such a tolerance towards minorities as that which is shown in Quebec.
An example of that is Three Rivers, very likely the most predominantly French city in America, where the English-speaking people, who do not make up more than 5 per cent of the population, have been given a wonderful school, very modern in design, and 90 per cent of its cost has been paid through direct provincial subsidies. It is a far cry from the scandalous happenings at Maillard-ville!
Mr. Speaker, when Quebec refuses federal subsidies and asks that a fair basis for the allocation of taxes be further considered, it does so in the best interests of the whole Canadian people.
What we need today is a federal-provincial conference which would draft a new and truly Canadian constitution, equal to the needs of a great modern nation.
But the government obviously does not want it; it is perfectly satisfied to leave Quebec isolated, with a financial status inferior to those of the other provinces.
The Budget-Mr. Shaw
When the calling of such a conference at the earliest possible moment is requested, the ministers suggest that to believe an agreement is in the least possible, is to deceive oneself. This is but a poor excuse, for one need only read the proceedings of the last two conferences, and particularly the speeches of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in which he commends all provincial premiers for their sincere co-operation and understanding.
This request for a new and essentially Canadian constitution, where the powers of everyone would be defined anew, does not come as a surprise to anyone. The speeches made by Liberals today are very remote from those with which they used to welcome the federal-provincial conferences. I remember the high praises then addressed to the Prime Minister.
I remember that government followers stated in fact that he would go down in history as the Prime Minister who "repatriated the constitution".
This conference has not been held now for three years. Has the Prime Minister decided not to repatriate the constitution? If he has so decided, why does he not come out and say so? If he has not, why has there been no conference for three years? Was it only an election pledge? Is it intended to be used anew next summer?
If the reports of the last two constitutional conferences are studied, it will be noted that the Prime Minister had only praise for the spirit of co-operation of the premier of Quebec.
On the other hand the Minister of Justice, at the end of the conference, stated that this meeting had given rise to great hopes and that success could not fail to attend the next one. But where is the Minister of Justice's optimism at this time? Whose fault is it if such a conference has not been held?
This decision is one man's work, and that man is the present Prime Minister of Canada. (Text) :

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) delivered what I considered to be a thought-provoking speech. Probably the Liberals would rather have it described as just a provoking speech. Certainly no hon. member could do better than commend that speech to the very serious consideration of all hon. members sitting on the Liberal side of the house.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw indicated the urgent necessity for economies in gov-
2548	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Shaw ernment. He underscored the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production as the fields in which we could effect very important and substantial economies, and do it in a hurry, if a proper course of action were followed. Many of us have felt very keenly to the same effect. On the basis of information we have, and with which other hon. members are familiar, we are not convinced that Canadians are securing full value for the dollars being spent for defence.
I suggest to the Liberals that the best thing they can do during the course of this debate is to give less consideration to minor tax cuts and more consideration to such vitally important matters as the effecting of economies in government fields of activity. When the Liberal ship cracks up on the reef it will be said that one of the principal reasons was the very things to which we have made reference, which have been characterized variously as extravagance, waste and the like.
This afternoon when the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) expropriated the time of the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith) -and perhaps "expropriated" is not the best word to use-I had expected the minister to deal with certain of those references made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. After hearing from the minister I felt a compelling urge to send a note to the hon. member for Moose Mountain offering him my time, although I would have had to assure him at the same time that I would expect more value for my time than he had received for his.
Much has been said about the so-called sunshine budget. After a long period of persistently stormy tax weather, through which the Canadian taxpayers have suffered, possibly it would be correct to conclude that a slight ray, just a glimmer, of sunshine did break through as a consequence of that budget. However, those storm clouds have not been completely dispelled; and judging by experiences of the past we can still expect much stormy weather from the government so far as taxation is concerned.
With the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) as skipper at the helm we can assume that, if the government gets by the reef known as an election, we will still have a rough passage. It is amazing to note how under a given set of circumstances he can reach certain conclusions at one time and, with the same set of circumstances, reach entirely different conclusions at another time. For example, can anyone feature the Minister of Finance reaching the conclusions which he did reach on February 19 a year ago or even two years ago with an election as far away as it would be then? Can anyone


feature the Minister of Finance reaching his February 19 conclusions next year or two years hence? Certainly I cannot. It is amazing what can be done with $50 million this pre-election year, and what could not be done a year or two years ago when the surplus was much more substantial. Can the Canadian taxpayer count on next year bringing such a so-called sunshine budget if the circumstances in the main are the same at that time as they are now? I think they cannot count on it.
One great reason for the difference is the fact that this must be regarded as an election year. Possibly this was the reason behind a constituent of mine writing to me recently urging that I sponsor a private bill which would have as its purpose amending the constitution to provide for an election every two years. It is conceivable that behind his thinking was the knowledge that strange things can be done in an election year when similar things cannot be done at other times, even under more favourable circumstances.
It was interesting for me to note that after all these years of experience in connection with the levying and collection of the radio licence fee it was finally learned that it is, and I use the minister's exact words, uneconomical to collect such a small individual fee from such a high proportion of Canadian families. The government knew that last year; the government knew that two years ago, but suddenly it has dawned upon them that it is uneconomical to collect such a small individual fee from so many Canadian families. This matter has been debated in this house year after year, and the government has always found good cause to retain this fee. I am not complaining that it has been abolished, as that action was certainly long overdue; but it needs an election year for some people to conclude that it is a wise course of action to pursue.
I hope the people of Canada are not going to be kidded too much in connection with this matter, because the C.B.C. will still be there with its mouth wide open, regulating and competing with the private stations and yet waiting for tremendous handouts. While those handouts may not come from licence fees designated as individual fees imposed upon individual families, they will come from the general treasury of the country.

The Budget-Mr. Shaw But when it ran into $20, $30, $40 or $50, as it does for too many families in this country, it becomes anything but normal. It is a matter of very keen regret to me- and this is not the first time I have brought this question before the house-that long before now the government has not given consideration to the removal of the sales tax on municipal purchases. It is a rather strange situation. Here is the municipal government serving the people within its field of jurisdiction in much the same manner as the provincial governments serve the people within their field of jurisdiction. There is an arrangement under which a concession is made to the provincial governments, but the municipal governments are compelled to pay.
In the past two arguments have been advanced in support of the government's stand. One relates to the loss of revenue. While there may have been some justifiable argument with respect to that aspect of the matter at one time, surely that same argument would not prevail today. Second, it has been argued that there is a serious administrative difficulty, but let us never forget that the United States has been able to solve whatever difficulty may have arisen. There is no problem at all so far as they are concerned with respect to administration.
Municipalities find it impossible to tax federal property. We know there is a provision whereby under certain circumstances, provided there is a certain amount of assessable property belonging to the federal government within the municipality, grants in lieu of taxes may be made, but most municipalities simply do not qualify under that provision. It is a matter of very keen disappointment to me that we have reached this stage without the federal government having found it possible to give favourable consideration with respect to this question. It would certainly alleviate the burden that our municipalities are bearing at this time, a burden created not by themselves but as a consequence of federal government policy.
This afternoon the hon. member for Anna-polis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) referred to a matter to which I should also like to make reference. It was brought up in the house before Christmas by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). I am not suggesting for a

The Budget-Mr. Shaw moment that farmers should not abide by the law. Certainly they should, but this is a strange procedure. A team of collectors, examiners, inspectors or whatever you want to call them move into my home town, for example; but prior to coming there they send notices to a certain number of farmers telling them that on such and such a day they must appear with their records.
Apparently this plan is to result eventually in complete coverage. They have not picked out these fellows because they suspect they have broken the law or have failed to make the declarations they should make. I have suggested to such farmers that they might try an experiment. I do not know what attitude the Department of National Revenue will take, but I think these farmers are justified in doing that.
The best judgment is certainly not exercised by these teams of men when they go out to conduct their examinations. They are anything but psychologists. I think some of them had better be given a little additional training. I realize of course that what is happening is not pleasing the Liberals any more than it is pleasing us. I am not looking at the question from a political point of view, because if there is political damage being done it is being done to the Liberals, and I would be encouraging it if that were my only motive. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not like the way these men conduct themselves. Where is the fairness? While I am not opposing doctors being allowed to deduct their expenses for attending conventions-

In the course of his budget speech the minister laid considerable emphasis upon debt reduction. According to the white paper tabled in the house Canada's estimated unmatured funded debt-it may even go beyond an estimate-will stand at March 31, 1953, at $14,837,630,437.68. The interest on that debt totals $409,456,495.84, the greater part of which is payable in Canada, part in New York and part in London. The minister emphasized the benefits of his $2,200 million debt reduction, as he calls it, but I have not been able to satisfy myself yet with respect to one aspect of it. 1 wonder whether this debt reduction actually resulted from the conviction on the part of the minister that debt reduction and the eventual elimination of debt is desirable, or whether it resulted from the fact that he was faced with a series of embarrassing surpluses accruing, as certain hon. members have

charged, from overtaxation. That might sound like a queer question until one examines the record of the banking and commerce committee of 1939. Mr. Graham Towers is the governor of the Bank of Canada, and Mr. Graham Towers, it is assumed, is one in whom the minister has great confidence and to whom the minister turns very frequently for advice. Mr. Graham Towers takes a very strange attitude towards the elimination of debt. He was asked in 1939, by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) in the banking and commerce committee:
Is It possible for you to imagine any way by which we are ever going to pay the debt we have got?
Mr. Towers answered:
As the debts of the government are an asset of the Canadian people I do not see much point in the thing; except that, to the extent that the government thinks that the distribution of those assets of the Canadian people-which are its debt-is unsatisfactory, it may take steps to remedy that distribution in any way that lies within the legislative power; in fact, in any way, I suppose.-by income tax or succession duties or any other action it cares to take.
This is another very interesting part of his answer:
So that all I can say would be this, that in a country where the sum total of public and private debt was decreasing you have a country which is going backward and which is becoming more poverty stricken. Generally speaking, in a country where you find there is no public and private debt you have a country resembling darkest Africa; there is nothing else.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I repeat my question of a moment ago. Did the minister's debt reduction result from a conviction on his part that it is desirable to reduce debt and eventually eliminate it, or did it result from a succession of what he found to be rather embarrassing surpluses which he quickly credited to debt reduction?
Well, I have always been led to believe that it is very desirable to reduce debt, if not eliminate it; but I also realize that under the system as we know it today Mr. Towers was probably absolutely right. I think one of the most difficult things that a Liberal government, following strictly orthodox policy, could be faced with would be the elimination of national and personal debt in this country.

He also referred to the fact that if the assets earned 5 per cent it would mean $290 million exported each year, with no corresponding imports. On February 27 it was pointed out by a government member that apparently the hon. member for Peace River had forgotten something. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) indicated that the hon. member for Peace River had apparently forgotten that a substantial amount of United States capital had been invested in Alberta's oil fields. Well, Mr. Speaker, that was true; but that capital came into Alberta substantially as a consequence of what? The failure on the part of Canadians to invest in that industry in the province of Alberta, and the failure of British financiers to invest in the oil industry of that province.
I well recall our former minister of lands and mines spending weeks in this part of Canada trying to bring about the investment of capital from central Canada. That was prior to 1947, when Leduc field came in. He Went overseas as well; and when it became obvious, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian and British capital had refused to invest in Alberta oil, United States capital was definitely invited to come in. Possibly those who opposed that action might change their tactics and tell us exactly how they would have handled the situation under similar circumstances. Would they have said, upon the failure of Canadian capital to invest, upon the failure of British capital to invest: We are just going to leave the industry undeveloped?
Well, Mr. Speaker, we certainly did not do that in my province. Those with money were invited in, but it was made abundantly clear to them that there would be hard and fast terms and conditions under which they would operate. They would have to bid for leases. If successful they would have to enter into contracts which were terminable if broken. They had to pay lease fees and royalties. Up to and including 1951 the oil companies actually did take $300 million out of the country. Only $190 million of that

The Budget-Mr. Shaw came from crown-owned lands over which the government of that province had no control; but of that $190 million the government of that province procured from fees, royalties, etc., $125 million, which was 66 per cent of actual production.
Mr. Speaker, there is no government in the world that has procured a larger percentage of the production of its oil industry for its people than has the government of the province of Alberta. There is no country anywhere where such proportional sums have been recovered for the people.

I mention this, Mr. Speaker, because of the fact that the hon. member for Peace River had said that some of this type of investment was desirable but certain types of foreign investment are not desirable. But of course if I were dealing with bonds as a type of foreign investment, I might have a different story to tell. I do not intend to pursue that any further, Mr. Speaker, except that I should like to say this in passing. speechtext: I cannot allow the hon. member to make that statement. He must withdraw it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I gladly withdraw it. Actually, sir, I saw the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Lesage) half rising before I said that, and I was just seeing if I could get him all the way up. The point I want to emphasize is this. I will not repeat what I said. With you, sir, I should like to believe I was wrong. The hon. member for Athabaska persists in making the statement that the farmer in Alberta who does not hold mineral rights does not get one cent. That is not a statement of fact. There is no farmer anywhere in Alberta who does not benefit from the industry. I do not want to be misunderstood in saying that. There is not a case in Alberta where a farmer, upon whose land there is drilling, gets nothing, whether he owns the mineral rights or whether he does not.
I could quote cases, as I have done before time and time again. Here is one farmer who did not own the mineral rights. This was a case in Redwater. There were four wells on his quarter section, and he did not own the mineral rights. He got $4,792 for the first year, and will get $1,586 for each subsequent year the wells are in operation. Here is the case of a farmer in the Millet district, who was awarded $840 for the first year and $380 for each subsequent year, with one well on his property. In each case the first payment is a cash payment. One could go on for hours citing cases. As I said on the floor of this house once before, we have the right-of-entry arbitration board in our province. A farmer definitely can stop an oil-drilling concern from entering upon his property, and can force them to go before the arbitration board, where an award will be made.
Some of these people desire to convey the impression that it would be fair if one per cent of the people of the province of Alberta-only about one-tenth hold mineral rights-were allowed to secure enormous returns from what might be discovered on their property, while 99 per cent of them are not afforded the same opportunity. The best way to acquire benefits for all the people of the province is under the policy we have out there.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I was amazed also that the hon. member for Athabaska would practically condemn the Alberta policy of setting up loans for self-liquidating projects from which municipalities can borrow funds at a very low rate of interest. In fact, he condemned a policy recently announced in that

province under which municipalities will be able to do their entire borrowing from similar funds set up by the provincial government.
I know the people of Alberta are not going to be very happy when they read what the hon. member for Athabaska said about that.
In the minute or two that is left to me I should like to say that reference has been made from time to time to the fact that there has been a decline in some prices. It seems rather unfortunate to me that, so far as agriculture generally is concerned, the major part of that decline has been in the livestock industry. From the information I have acquired, and which has already been put on this record, it seems to me that the income from farm production in 1952 is approximately $1,900 million, representing a very substantial drop in net earnings from the previous year. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) said it was high time some action was taken by this parliament to institute an investigation into the cost of farm machinery. The farmer would be prepared to see his prices falling providing his cost of production or the cost of the things he has to buy was falling at the same time. But to be faced with a situation where his income is falling while the costs of machinery, services, wages and so forth are mounting, is unbearable.
It seems to me most unfair that the burden should fall upon that group within our country, while the net rental income from interest is increasing; while government investment is showing increased returns; while corporation profits have remained about the same; while the net income of non-farm corporate business remains substantially unchanged. It seems unfair that the farmer should be subjected to a substantial loss of anywhere from 12 to 14 per cent in 1952 as compared with 1951. In my own area, which is a cattle area, the drop in farm income has varied from about 20 to 25 per cent. It is true that the opening of the United States market may have a beneficial effect, but let us not forget that it could also have the reverse effect since the Mexican, market has also been opened.
In conclusion may I say I am personally convinced that the time has now come when the government should see fit to call an election just as soon as they can possibly do so.
