Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to express my appreciation of the honour that was given me in having been chosen to represent the constituency of Richelieu-Vercheres in this house. I also want to express the pleasure I feel in being associated with all the members of this house, and in working with them. I do not imagine that I need to go into any detail in expressing what I may feel as a new member. I rather imagine that all hon. members still recall with what timidity they looked upon the profound political knowledge of their colleagues. So, Mr. Speaker, this speech cannot be more than perhaps an expression of the impressions and the sincere opinions of a new member.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speeches from both sides of the house, but I have paid particular attention to the criticisms that have been levelled at the government by the members of the opposition. Although the opposition has no administrative powers, although it has no responsibility, and although it does little but criticize, it is not itself above serious criticism. In its criticism of government policy the opposition invariably neglects to make mention of anjt problems that the government has to face, and for which they have to find a solution, with respect to any of their legislation. The opposition will take a particular measure away from all the conditions or circumstances that may have a direct bearing on it and will criticize the thing in itself without looking around to see what were the factors that forced the government to act in a par-


ticular way. The fact that the opposition does not consider any of the problems involved leaves them with a free hand to make interesting and popular-sounding speeches, by having things both ways. No government, Mr. Speaker, can have things both ways; and no serious government can afford to leave out of any discussion in this house any of the problems that the government has to face. If the opposition wants to be fair it cannot but make mention of these problems and take them into consideration.
I was saying that the opposition wanted things both ways. For example, Hansard is full of speeches by members of the opposition demanding an increase in practically all the social measures; and there are an equal number of speeches from members of the opposition demanding a reduction in taxes. The opposition speaks of the urgent need of maintaining the national defence program, and it also speaks in favour of redistributing the very taxes that make this national defence program possible. The opposition speaks of the autonomy of the provinces and of the wrong principle being followed in a centralized government. At the same time, however, it speaks in favour of adopting legislation that has to do with the exclusive provincial rights of the various provinces, such as in the field of education, labour, etc. It is simple, Mr. Speaker, to touch the hearts of the people by making speeches in such a way; but one cannot do that, I submit, without running the grave risk of being considered most illogical.
No government can have things both ways, and no government can ignore the problems. Some of the most important ones are, for instance, the social security measures. I do not intend here to repeat all that has been said in this house on social security measures; it resembles a broken record, it has been repeated so many times. But I should like to mention the fact that all the social security measures that now exist in Canada have been the creation of this government. This government is therefore aware that there is a social need, and would be the first to increase all the social security measures if it were possible. But on the other hand, Mr. Speaker, this government cannot speak only of social security measures; it has to put them into effect. That means finding the ways and means of doing it; and, as you know, that can be done only by having the people themselves contribute.
A short time ago I read an interesting article in the Ottawa Journal of January 2, 1953, entitled: "Cost of 'Social Security'", which reads in part as follows:
Mr. Paul Martin said In the House of Commons the other day that the estimated expenditure of

public funds (that is of tax money) on "social security" in Canada for the current fiscal year will be $1,349,100,000. Of that enormous total the dominion government will pay $1,010,500,000, the provincial governments $255,400,000 and the municipal governments $83,200,000 . . .
In other words, on the three levels of government there is being collected through taxes close to $100 a year from every man, woman and child in Canada for social security, which means for family allowances, old age pensions, unemployment relief, aid for distressed individuals and families in the many forms it takes.
The Journal does not suggest that too much is being done or that it is being done wastefully and extravagantly. It does seem, however, that all of us should realize what social security is costing us and should understand the necessity of moving slowly in making new commitments.
That, Mr. Speaker, has been the policy of this government. It is not merely a question of introducing in legislation new or increased social measures. They not only have to be adopted, they have to be maintained; and they have to be maintained in periods of peace as well as in periods of war, and despite any crisis, and despite also the increasing demands of the Canadian public. All these questions have to be taken into account before any reasonable solution can be had, if we are to consider the economic security of this country.
In the past few days we have listened to innumerable speeches from the opposition criticizing the 1953 budget. To some it was a thoroughly bad budget; to others it was so good that the government had adopted it just because it was an election year. But on the other hand, no one said what it actually was, a necessary budget based upon the demands of the Canadian people; and that it was also the continuation of an economic policy that has been loudly applauded by all the leading economists throughout the world.
I had the opportunity of putting my hands on an address that was prepared by the late Dr. W. C. Clark, who was deputy minister of finance. It was supposed to have been delivered at a joint meeting of the American economic association, the American finance association and the Chicago association of commerce and industry, on December 29, 1952. I am only sorry I cannot go through the whole of the address, because I think it is one of the most enlightening I have ever read. At this time I can give only an inadequate outline of what he said. He pointed out that the economics of a country is not something that can be brought up and down, like an elevator, as it were, to suit any purpose. Any serious government has to consider all the problems involved in the economic set-up of its country.
The Budget-Mr. Cardin
At that particular conference the late Dr. Clark would have shown exactly what those problems were, and what the solutions were that have made possible the prosperity we now enjoy. If hon. members will recall, the war had cost $20 billion; and even though the financial policy during the war was as rigorous as that of any other belligerent nation, the national debt increased from $3 [DOT] 2 billion to $13-4 billion.
Industry at the same time had so greatly expanded for war purposes that the national production potential had been greatly augmented, and the government was faced with the problem of integrating a large war plant capacity into the peacetime economy. The government had to find employment for about a million and a half war civilian workers, and demobilized service personnel. Canada's normal production in time of peace represented from 20 to 25 per cent of its total wartime production. After the war the government was worried about the destruction that had taken place in the countries with which Canada normally traded. It was also greatly worried about the breakdown in the multilateral system of trade and payments. These were the problems with which the government was faced, and about which we hear nothing from hon. members on the other side of the house.
How can anyone suggest any solution to a problem without first delving deeply into those problems? Also it might be well to recall at this time that at the lowest point of the depression in 1933 our production had fallen to $3-6 billion. In 1939 it had climbed back to $5-7 billion. In 1945 it stood at $11-9 billion; and today it is more than $23 billion.
The opposition, of course, calls this rapid expansion a war boom. As a matter of fact it is still waiting for the depression that was predicted six or seven years ago. Unfortunately the opposition will be disappointed, because this is not a war boom. This expansion was purposely balanced; and as a matter of fact the increase in Canada in the field of industry is common to industries throughout all Canada, and there are no excesses or distortions such as are prevalent in all war booms.
This is made very clear if one considers what caused the rapid economic expansion in Canada. The war itself of course was a great factor, with all its new industries, qualified technicians and production machinery. Then there was another important factor, in the growth of population which came about through natural increase, as well as by a more vigorous immigration policy and by the accession of Newfoundland. Since 1939 the population of Canada has been augmented to the extent of 28 per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Cardin
Another important factor was the wide search for hidden riches with the use of all our modern equipment. There was no longer any prospecting with the aid of a mule and a hammer with which one would knock once in a while on a rock. There was the new magnetometer, and other instruments; and with those instruments, and the will of the Canadian people, there were huge discoveries in the Laurentian field, in the Appalachian field, in the Rocky mountains and on the plains of Alberta. These included nickel, copper, zinc, cobalt, uranium, asbestos and oil; and most important in this expansion were the vast sums of money that were spent on new capital investment. In 1946 new capital investment was 14-2 per cent of our national product; in 1951 it came up to 21-6 per cent, and in 1952 it was 23 per cent of our national product. And this new capital investment is responsible for the employment of 800,000 people, representing 15 per cent of our total labour force.
There is no war boom; and it was only because the government had the foresight to control development in the industrial field to such an extent that it avoided all the excesses that might have come about. At the close of the war the government was aware of this natural development, and it adopted a definite policy. It did not leave anything to chance, as the opposition have claimed. It adopted a definite policy that was designed, first of all, for a smooth transition from a war economy to a peacetime economy. It endeavoured to restore and maintain a free enterprise economy. It tried to promote a rising level of employment and income. It adopted a policy to avoid inflation, particularly at the outbreak of the Korean war when our national production was already under stress from the expanding economy that had taken place in Canada in previous years.
Those problems were the same as those faced by any large nation, such as the United States. It was not chance that made us succeed more than they did. Even the Americans themselves are aware of that particular fact which was indicated by an editorial in the Daily News of June 10, 1952, entitled "Oh, Canada-How do you do it?" and which reads:
We hope none of the readers missed Robert Conway's June 8 Sunday News report on Canada and why its dollar, for the first time in history, is worth more than ours.
The humiliating upset is only a dramatic part of a larger picture. That picture includes Canadian government encouragement of private enterprise, farming out of government powers to provincial (state) officials instead of hogging them in the dominion capital city of Ottawa, firing useless public payrollers, and in various other ways firmly refusing to imitate the U.S. fair deal.


We move that Truman & Co., using the Conway report as a guide and blueprint, send a commission to Ottawa to find out more-much more- about how Canada does it. This would involve a feat of pride-pocketing of which, frankly, we don't think the fair dealers are capable. But it would also dig up a barrel of useful tips and information which the people of the United States badly need. What ho, Harry?
That is the attitude of the United States people toward our economic policy. How did the government do it? It did it by organizing the industrial development bank to furnish necessary funds for new sound enterprises and to furnish capital for existing enterprises. It adopted the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It organized the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It set up the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. It authorized the Minister of Finance to grant export credits, and as a matter of fact $1-25 billion were loaned to the United Kingdom. In that way Canadian industry was able to convert to a peacetime economy with a rapidity that astounded everyone.
This is the whole scheme of things which the opposition is criticizing so strongly; and under it, it was necessary to have taxation. Although hon. members of the opposition do not seem to realize it, the budget forms part of the nation's business. It has an influence on and is influenced by employment, income and prices. The taxation policy must be decided in the light of the economic problems to be solved.
When we look at the question of taxation we should consider that after the war the government was faced with a dilemma. The necessarily high taxes of wartime had impaired and weakened our national production, and at that time we had to maintain the maximum effort in that particular field if we were going to keep our economy on a sound basis. That was one argument for reducing taxes.
On the other hand, there was a good argument for maintaining the high tax rate because it was a good thing for the country to pay off its national debt when it could do so. It must be remembered that we had spent $20 billion during the war. By having budgetary surpluses the inflationary pressure caused by deferred demands and the great volume of liquid purchasing power could be checked. Those were the two horns of the dilemma upon which the government found itself, the one in favour of raising taxes and the other in favour of lowering them.
What did the government do? The government followed a happy medium; it adopted the golden rule. It reduced taxes in order to promote national production, and it did it in such a way as to allow a sufficient surplus with which to pay off the national debt

and in a particular way help to avoid the tendency toward inflation which was so predominant throughout the world.
Then as time went on and the surplus was sufficient to look after its needs, the government started to reduce taxes. The excess profits tax was first reduced and then repealed in 1947. I might say here that 1947 was not an election year. The corporate income tax was reduced from 40 per cent to 30 per cent in 1946, again not an election year. Personal income tax rates were cut successively in 1946 and 1947, and they were not election years. They were cut again in 1949, not because 1949 was an election year but because it was part of a program being followed by the government. Since 1946 the total reduction in taxes has amounted to 70 per cent for the great majority of taxpayers. In 1949 taxes were back to their normal prewar rates and Canada was enjoying the prosperity which still exists.
The Budget-Mr. Cardin
Then in 1950 came the Korean war. Members of the opposition have told us that we lowered taxes in 1949 and then put them up again in 1950. Why do they not consider the Korean war? The government did, and the government had to provide for an immense defence effort in order to look after the national safety of the country. Those are arguments that stand up, and it is high time that the opposition gave some real reasons for the fluctuations in taxation.
